PM Tarique’s Khulna visit brings big promises for industry, jobs
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday unveiled plans to develop an industrial corridor stretching from Mongla in the southwest to Panchagarh in the north, seeking to revive struggling industrial regions, attract investment and create employment through expanded port facilities, energy infrastructure and improved connectivity.
During a daylong visit to Bagerhat and Khulna, he laid the foundation stone of a Tk4,068 crore project to expand and modernise Mongla Port, witnessed the signing of an investment cooperation agreement with a Chinese state-owned company and pledged to reopen closed factories while encouraging the establishment of new industries.
The prime minister also assured workers that a new minimum wage would be fixed within one or two months, as garment workers continued demonstrations across several industrial areas demanding higher pay.
Addressing a roadside meeting at Katakhali intersection on the Khulna-Mongla highway, Tarique said his government wanted to restore Khulna’s former industrial prominence and extend industrial development across Bagerhat, Kushtia, Chuadanga and other districts towards Panchagarh.
He said the government would gradually develop the necessary electricity, gas and transport infrastructure to attract factories and generate employment along the proposed corridor.
Earlier, the prime minister laid the foundation stone of the Tk4,068 crore Mongla Port expansion and modernisation project, which includes two container jetties and supporting infrastructure to increase cargo-handling capacity and improve services.
Speaking at the ceremony, he described Mongla as a potential economic hub for the country’s southwestern and northwestern regions.
He said modernising the port would help expand trade and industrial activities in Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira and Jashore while strengthening economic connectivity with northern districts.
The government also plans to improve road links between Panchagarh and Mongla, expand port supply chains and facilitate cargo transportation.
According to the prime minister’s deputy press secretary, the project would enable direct container train services between Kamalapur Inland Container Depot in Dhaka and Mongla Port once the necessary facilities are operational.
Tarique also identified the development and operation of Khan Jahan Ali Airport as a government priority.
He stressed that the project’s success would depend not merely on completing infrastructure but also on reducing cargo-handling costs, improving efficiency and attracting investment.
At Mongla Port, the prime minister witnessed the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Invest Bangladesh and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) on economic and infrastructure cooperation.
Invest Bangladesh Member (Industrial Zones) Saleh Ahmed and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation Chairman Li Chongyang signed the agreement.
The cooperation framework covers potential investment in energy, industrial and environmentally sustainable infrastructure, transport, logistics and human resource development.
Tarique later held discussions with a Chinese delegation led by CRCC Chairman Dai Hegen.
He urged Chinese investors to establish industries around Mongla and emphasised the importance of reliable electricity and gas supplies for industrial expansion.
The prime minister also thanked the Chinese delegation for supporting opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to secure employment with Chinese companies in the Middle East.
The prime minister said the government wanted to reopen closed mills and factories, including state-owned establishments, and encourage domestic and foreign investment to create employment.
Later, he visited the shrine of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali in Bagerhat, where he offered prayers.
In Khulna, he inaugurated the second season of Notun Kuri Sports at the district stadium, highlighting the importance of sports, arts and cultural activities alongside academic education.
He said the government was committed to fulfilling its election promises and developing the next generation through education and extracurricular activities.
Around 1.6 million children are participating in the nationwide sporting initiative, according to the program details provided.
The prime minister also reiterated that his government would continue efforts to strengthen the economy despite global challenges.

item.title: Historic leadership firsts for minorities across US in midterm vote
item.description:
The US midterm vote ushered in a wave of historic leadership firsts across the country on Tuesday, electoral milestones on a night that saw voters issue a sharp rejection of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator, the first Muslim senator and the first female Native American governor all won groundbreaking elections in the vote that racked up resounding gains for Democrats.
Bill Shiebler -- chief strategy officer at the non-profit State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity -- told AFP the night was “a huge rebuke against hate and division.”
“We’re witnessing an electorate that increasingly sees itself in its leaders, and the leaders who come out of communities they now represent,” Shiebler said.
In Michigan, leftist Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
The former medical administrator drew huge campaign crowds but faced a surge of anti-Muslim rhetoric from his detractors in the bruising race.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations advocacy group praised El-Sayed for persevering despite “endless Islamophobic attacks.”
“Our communities worked hard to make sure our voices were heard and that we are properly represented in the Senate,” the organization said.
“This is what is possible when we show up and vote together.”
In the southern state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the race for governor, making her the first Black woman elected to the top office in any US state.
A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, a win that returns the governor’s office to Democrats after more than two decades of Republican control.
Democratic Representative Chris Pappas, meanwhile, will become the first openly gay man to serve in the US Senate after winning in New Hampshire. He has served in the US House of Representatives since 2019.
“No one should be discriminated against because of who they are or who they love,” he said on his website.
In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor, beating Republican Gregg Hull.
A member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe, she had served as the secretary of the interior under former president Joe Biden, the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary.
Democrat Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota was elected as the first female Native American senator.
The sweeping midterm rebuke of Trump also saw a number of state-level electoral firsts, including the first Latina governor in Texas with Gina Hinojosa’s victory.
Looking ahead, if the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wins the speakership as expected in the new Congress, he would become the first Black speaker of the House in US history.
“This was a historic election where people decided to believe in themselves and really lean into the hope about the promise of this country, rebuking an effort to snuff out people’s voices,” Shiebler said.

item.title: Health minister: Five Dhaka hospitals to launch PPP-based healthcare services
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Thursday said the government plans to launch improved healthcare services under a public-private partnership (PPP) model, initially at five hospitals in Dhaka on a trial basis.
“Plans are underway to expand the healthcare program to other cities,” he said while addressing an event held at Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Medical College Hospital (SZMCH) in Bogra.
The health minister said discussions with the five hospitals had been finalised, but another meeting would be held next week to determine the fees private partners would charge. The pilot program would begin once financial arrangements were settled, he added.
"We will initially introduce the program on a trial basis at five hospitals in Dhaka before expanding it to other cities. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is interested in the initiative, and we are working to implement it," he said.
Describing SZMCH as a major healthcare centre for northern Bangladesh, the minister said the government was considering expanding access to advanced treatment for complex diseases, including cancer and liver conditions.
Hospital authorities had been asked to submit written lists of their problems, which would be addressed gradually, he added.
On the shortage of doctors and the absence of a separate paediatric ICU at SZMCH, the minister said the government planned to establish around 20 new ICUs across the country, including one in Bogra. He said 17 of the 500 newly appointed doctors had been posted to different healthcare facilities in Bogra, with more appointments planned.
Recruitment of another 5,000 doctors is also underway. Applications have closed, and the Public Service Commission is conducting the interview process, he added.
Blaming corruption and mismanagement over the past 17 years for the deterioration of the healthcare sector, he said the current government was working to restore discipline and improve services.

item.title: QS Asia Rankings: DU retains top position from Bangladesh, 16th in South Asia
item.description:
Dhaka University has retained its position as the top university in Bangladesh in the QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027, securing 136th place among Asian universities and 16th among those in South Asia.
The UK-based international higher education and research organization Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) published the rankings on November 3. DU also held the top position among Bangladeshi universities in last year's rankings.
According to a press release issued by DU, a total of 1,722 universities from 26 countries across Asia have been included in this year's rankings. The University of Hong Kong secured the first position, followed by Peking University of China.
The QS Asia University Rankings assess universities based on several indicators, including academic reputation, faculty-student ratio, research quality and impact, the proportion of staff holding PhD degrees, international research collaboration, and the number of international faculty members and students.
DU Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr ABM Obaidul Islam expressed his satisfaction over the university's position in the international rankings. "This position in the international rankings is a matter of joy and pride for us. Consistently retaining the top position among Bangladeshi universities is recognition of collective efforts of our teachers, students, researchers and all concerned," he said.
However, he said the university's goal was not merely to maintain its ranking but to further strengthen its position internationally through improvement in the quality of education and research.
The vice-chancellor said enriching the academic and research environment, expanding research facilities, strengthening international collaborations and creating opportunities for students to develop globally competitive skills were among the university's key priorities.

'Effective altruism' is about finding the most effective ways to help others
item.description:
Peter Singer is known as the “world’s most influential living philosopher." This Australian moral philosopher, author and public intellectual is the co-founder of 'The Life You Can Save', 'The School for Moral Ambition' and 'Profit for Good'. Currently, he is the Professor of Bioethics, Emeritus, at Princeton University. Peter Singer recently was in Bangladesh to visit various development programmes of Brac, as well as Aarong and Brac University.

In an interview with Prothom Alo's Ayesha Kabir, he spoke about how the plight of Bangladesh's refugees during the 1971 Liberation War sparked his thinking about helping people in extreme poverty. He explained his concept of "effective altruism," about changing the norms of ethical behaviour, and more.  

Welcome to Bangladesh. How has your time here been so far?

Peter Singer: Thank you. I've had a very interesting time. I've learned a lot. It's been a very busy two or three days.

You are known as one of the world's most influential living philosophers. You often use the term "effective altruism". Can you elaborate on this term? What does it mean?

Peter Singer: The idea of altruism is reasonably familiar. An altruist is somebody who does things for others, not only for themselves. And the effective altruism movement doesn't expect people to be saints. It doesn't expect them to think only about others. It is about generally trying to make the world a better place. This should be an aim shared by all.

Secondly, we all have limited resources to do good for others, even Bill Gates. So when we have limited resources, we normally want to get the best value from those resources that we can. If you need a new phone and you only have a certain amount to spend, you will try to find the best phone for the money you have. But when it comes to giving to charity, most people have not applied the same standard. They have not done research into where they can do tThe effective altruism movement is about generally trying to make the world a better place. This should be an aim shared by allhe most good with what they're prepared to donate, whether it's money, time or skills, to altruism. So the "effective altruism" movement says it's very important to find the most effective ways you can help others, because the difference between less effective and more effective ways is huge.

There are charities that genuinely are trying to do something, but they just haven't found the most cost-effective way to use their resources. So effective altruism puts those two things together.

How did you reach this philosophy about effective altruism?

Peter Singer: My line of thought is about our responsibility for helping people in extreme poverty. We're talking about people who have money. After meeting their basic needs, they still have money to spend on luxuries. I wrote an article in the context of the Bangladesh War of Liberation, called Famine, Affluence and Morality. I wrote it in 1971. It was published in 1972. I started off with the fact that there were 9 million refugees from what was then East Pakistan who had fled across the border into India. India was struggling to meet that enormous need for food, shelter and sanitation.

I was at that time a graduate student at the University of Oxford, studying philosophy, and particularly ethics. I started thinking about what my ethical responsibilities were in this situation.

So I came up with this example, which has become quite famous. It is about walking past a shallow pond in which a small child has fallen, and the child is in danger of drowning. There's nobody else around the pond. You can save the child, but you will ruin your shoes and have to replace them. Would it be wrong of you to ignore the child and walk past the pond because you didn't want to spend money on a new pair of shoes? Obviously, people would say that would be a terrible thing to do.

But I argued that, in the situation of the refugees in India, most people in the affluent world were not doing anything about it. And even though the refugees were far away and you couldn't actually see them in front of you, it was ethically a similar situation. For a modest sum of money, you could quite possibly save a life and certainly contribute, together with others, to saving many lives. And that was what we ought to do.

That article got reprinted many times. A lot of students read it, and a lot of professors used it in their classes. Some decades later, some students decided that they wanted to found an organisation that would try to make this idea better known. They did some research on how big the differences might be between the best use of your money to help people and just an average kind of use of your money. So the emphasis was on quantification and assessment, using evidence to determine where you should put your money.

You mentioned the refugees in 1971. You must be aware that right now in Bangladesh we have a large number of refugees from Myanmar. International funds drying up. What would your message be about this particular situation?

Peter Singer: It's a very difficult situation. Obviously, what we would want to say is: allow the refugees to work and eventually give them a path to citizenship. But I understand that the government is worried that if they do that, they will get more refugees, and Bangladesh is already quite a densely populated country. So I understand that it's not easy. Somehow, there needs to be some assurance that this will not lead to a larger number of refugees coming across the border.

You were talking about this divide between the ultra-rich and the extremely poor. Would it be unrealistic to expect the ultra-rich to make a significant difference to poverty? Your ideas are very doable, but why isn't it being done? Are people simply selfish and uncaring?

Peter Singer: I don't think the rich are all the same. There are some rich people who have given away an immense amount of money. Bill and Melinda Gates set up the Gates Foundation. Warren Buffett is another super-rich person who gave a lot of his money away, and there are others, too, who have supported effective altruism causes. Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, who have made a lot of money in IT, are giving away most of their fortune, too, and they're actually funding a lot of research into finding the best ways to help people get out of poverty.

As I said, I don't think all the rich are the same, but unfortunately, you're right about the majority of them. And, of course, the most conspicuous and richest man in the world at the moment is definitely not an effective altruist.

We just have to keep trying to change the norms of ethical behaviour. Unfortunately, we have some leaders who are setting very bad examples in terms of ethical behaviour. We have some internet influencers who are the same. But I'm in touch with a lot of people who are doing very ethical things through the effective altruism movement. So I don't think you can say that everybody has suddenly become selfish. That is certainly not true.

Bangladesh has made a lot of progress and lifted a large majority of its population out of extreme poverty. So I think Bangladesh's story is actually an inspiring one

So you do think that you and like-minded people can really make an impact?

Peter Singer: Almost anybody can make some impact if they can find the most effective organisations. I set up this organisation called 'The Life You Can Save', which recommends the most effective charities helping people in extreme poverty. So they can easily get that information and they can find that they can make a big difference without being particularly rich.

If you choose the right charities, they're very effective, and you will find it rewarding.

Institutions like BRAC and various other charities around the world can do a lot, but it is the governments that make policies. Do you think governments also need to be influenced to work in a similar direction?

Peter Singer: Yes, they do. Unfortunately, governments are not living up to their responsibilities now. The example set by the United States is a very poor one, particularly in recent times. And other governments are saying, well, if the United States is going to slash its overseas aid, we'll do the same. So that's a very bad example to follow.

I'm also advocating that companies do more to donate profits, or some of their profits, to good causes. I've recently co-founded something called the Profit for Good Alliance, which is an alliance of companies that give at least 10 per cent of their profits to good causes. We want to publicise them. We want to try to get consumers to prefer them. We want to spread the idea that just earning profits is not enough. You need to use at least some of that to make a positive difference.

There is a website you can look at called profitforgood.com. It's not officially launched. We're going to have a big conference in Europe next June to launch it.

What about the United Nations, which was ostensibly formed to make a difference in such situations. Has it become totally dysfunctional?

Peter Singer: No, I don't think the UN is totally dysfunctional, but it has been ignored by some world leaders. It was obviously ignored by Putin when he invaded Ukraine. And it seems that Trump has also been ignoring it. On a smaller scale, the capture of Maduro in Venezuela was a pretty flagrant violation of the UN Charter, and on a larger scale, I think the war with Iran. There was no real necessity for that war. The negotiations should have been continued. War must always be an absolute last resort. You can't say that the US and Israel's attack on Iran was an absolute last resort at all.

What about UN organisations like UNICEF, UNDP and UNESCO. In terms of the amount of funding they're getting, do you think they're spending it effectively?

Peter Singer: None of those organisations you mentioned are on 'The Life You Can Save' list of the most effective charities. They do a lot of different things, and some of those things are good, but I don't think that everything they do is good. They're not as close to the local people as BRAC is, for example. I think one of the things about BRAC from the start was that it sought to learn from local people what they wanted and gain knowledge from them.

Lastly, what message would you like to leave for Bangladesh?

Peter Singer: As I said, Bangladesh was at the start of my thinking about poverty. A lot of people had very gloomy predictions about the future of Bangladesh as an independent nation. And those gloomy predictions have not come true. On the contrary, Bangladesh has made a lot of progress and lifted a large majority of its population out of extreme poverty. So I think Bangladesh's story is actually an inspiring one, which should give people hope and encouragement to continue working towards ending large-scale extreme poverty everywhere in the world.

Thank you. That's a positive note to end on.

Peter Singer: Thank you.

item.title: Applied Human Science College students block Nilkhet road demanding principal’s resignation
item.description:
Students of Government College of Applied Human Science (formerly Home Economics College) in the capital continued their protests for a second consecutive day, demanding the resignation of Principal Professor Meherun Nessa and justice over an alleged police attack on students, among other demands.

The students began protesting after blocking both sides of the road in front of the college in Nilkhet shortly after 10:30 am today, Friday. Traffic came to a standstill as a result.

The protesting students said they would continue their movement, until their demands were met. However, none of them agreed to speak on record, giving their names and identities.

At around 10:30 am yesterday, Thursday, students began a sit-in in front of the principal’s office. At one point, they confined her inside the office. Police arrived at around 11:30 pm and rescued her. The protesters alleged that police baton-charged students at the time. Several students were injured in the incident.

Officer-in-charge (OC) of Lalbagh Police Station Mohammad Jamil Hossain told Prothom Alo this morning that more than 50 students had blocked the road in front of the college and were staging protests. They were chanting various slogans, including calls for the principal’s resignation. However, no untoward incident has occurred there, he said.

The protesters’ demands include the resignation of Principal Professor Meherun Nessa, the issuance of show-cause notices to police officers who allegedly beat students with batons inside the campus, the indefinite suspension of all campus activities until the principal submits a written resignation, and a declaration that teachers and employees who tried to justify the attack are unwelcome on campus.

At around 10:30 am yesterday, Thursday, students began a sit-in in front of the principal’s office. At one point, they confined her inside the office. Police arrived at around 11:30 pm and rescued her. The protesters alleged that police baton-charged students at the time. Several students were injured in the incident.

CUET VC says he has not resigned; teachers and students vow to continue protest

In protest, students also staged demonstrations on the road in front of the college last night. Today, they have taken to the streets again for the second day.

According to protesting students and college administration sources, before the Puja holidays, a farewell programme was organised at the college auditorium for final-year postgraduate students from five departments across three residential halls.

Initially, the programme was scheduled to end by 10:00 pm. At the students’ request, the deadline was later extended to midnight. However, the programme did not end until 5:00 am.

As the auditorium was used beyond the permitted time, Principal Meherun Nessa cancelled the residential hall seats of two students who had coordinated the programme.

When the students later went to apologise, they were told that their seats would be reinstated on condition that they paid a fine of Tk 12,600 to cover the auditorium’s air-conditioning and electricity costs for one night. The students launched their protest in response.

The principal also said, “They are asking me to sign a resignation letter on a blank sheet of paper. Why should I resign to them?”

While she was confined inside her office yesterday evening, Principal Meherun Nessa told journalists, “What the students are saying is totally the opposite of what happened. I had given them permission to hold a programme until midnight. They continued until 5:00 am. As a result, I got a little angry and cancelled the hall seats of two of them.”

“Later, they apologised to me. I showed some leniency and told them that, since they had not maintained any discipline, they would have to face disciplinary action to ensure order in the future. They wasted electricity for a long time, and I will collect that bill from them. I issued the notice imposing the fine, and that is my offence,” she added.

The principal also said, “They are asking me to sign a resignation letter on a blank sheet of paper. Why should I resign to them?”

item.title: Russell Brand guilty of rape, three sexual assaults
item.description:
BRITAIN-COURT/BRAND

British comedian Russell Brand was on Thursday found guilty by a London jury of one rape and three sexual assaults, involving a total of four women.

Brand, who closed his eyes but showed no emotion as the jury delivered the verdicts, was cleared of two rapes and one count of attempted indecent assault against two other women.

Judge Joel Bennathan warned the 51-year-old actor turned conservative religious online guru that he faced a "significant custodial term".

Brand's wife Laura, who has accompanied him most days since the start of the trial on 12 October, watched from the public gallery as the jury at London's Southwark Crown Court delivered their four unanimous guilty verdicts.

He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced on Monday. The maximum sentence in the UK for rape is life imprisonment.

Brand, who was briefly married to US popstar Katy Perry, also faces a further accusation of raping two more women, including a 16-year-old schoolgirl, and could face further criminal charges.

The allegations, which are being investigated by the Metropolitan Police and could not be reported earlier, were revealed at previous hearings of his four-week trial.

A Met spokesperson said in a statement sent to AFP that Brand had "been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations" but declined to confirm the women's ages.

After the verdicts, the Met paid tribute to the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward".

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," the Met's Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said in a statement.

"As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be," Furphy added.

Ahead of the trial, Brand's defence team attempted to get the case dismissed on the grounds that a 2023 documentary and newspaper article making separate, anonymised allegations about Brand meant he had been convicted "in the court of the media of being a rapist".

Russell Brand accused of sexual assault on set of 'Arthur' in 2010

But the judge ruled it was sufficient to eliminate jurors who remembered seeing this coverage, which prompted police to investigate Brand.

Police released videos of interviews with Brand during the investigation where he read out prepared statements slamming the "defamatory and fictitious documentary" which he said resulted in further encounters being "invented or reimagined".

'Insatiable'

Senior prosecutor David Roberts said outside the court Thursday that Brand was "predatory and used his celebrity status to commit sexual crimes".

"He was a manipulator with an insatiable desire to get what he wanted regardless of whether consent was given or not," Roberts added.

Brand was convicted of four sexual offences -- one rape and three sexual assaults -- involving four women between 2005 and 2009 in different locations, including a radio station, a recording studio and Brand's home address.

He had pleaded not guilty to all the charges saying that although he used to be very promiscuous he had always had consensual sex.

Following the guilty verdicts, Brand's lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to renew his bail over the weekend as "an act of humanity".

Winter said he was asking for bail so Brand could "put his affairs in order and in particular to say goodbye to his three young children".

Judge Bennathan said he regretted the "hardship caused to the children".

But he said Brand had "considerable resources" and that whatever his good intentions were there were substantial grounds to "fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence".

From the dock, Brand signalled to his defence team that he was okay, adding: "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good" before being led out of the dock.

Brand's wife Laura later left the court building wearing dark glasses and was hurried into a car by a bodyguard.

item.title: Chinese citizens making live videos from morning till night, even going inside people’s homes
item.description:
A group of foreign nationals are seen walking around the streets, each carrying two mobile phones. One phone is being used to livestream, while something is written on the screen of the other. At first glance, one might assume they are journalists or working on Google Street View. But that is not the case. They have been livestreaming in this manner for months. Their broadcasts run from morning until night. At times, they even enter people's homes and record videos. This has left local residents confused.

Such activities by Chinese nationals can be seen in Sector 12 of Uttara and the Tekpara area of Dhaka. However, no accurate information is available on how many Chinese nationals are involved in recording these videos in the area. 

Local residents estimate that more than 150 Chinese nationals are filming in this manner in the neighbourhood's streets and alleyways. However, residents have no idea where these videos are published or what is being said in them. Not even the local police station monitors their activities. What initially sparked curiosity among residents—the practice of livestreaming from morning until night—has now become a source of growing irritation.

Akram Hossain, a resident of the Tekpara area in Uttara, told Prothom Alo: “It would be understandable if this were just a matter of a day or two. But they (the Chinese nationals) have been making these videos for months. They start filming before we even wake up. When we go to bed, we still see them filming. But we have no idea what they do with these videos.”

Where do the videos go?

The activities of Chinese nationals in Uttara have sparked curiosity among local residents. Even newcomers to the area are somewhat surprised by what they see and want to know why these people are making videos. They wonder why ordinary daily activities are being filmed in this way, even though the area has no particularly notable attractions for visitors.

Local residents say Chinese nationals livestream from various parts of Uttara, but they do so most frequently in the Tekpara area. A canal runs alongside Sector 12 of Uttara, and Tekpara is situated on its banks. Compared with other parts of Uttara, the area is less developed and predominantly inhabited by low-income people. Due to its dense population, the neighbourhood is also quite dirty. It is precisely this area that the Chinese nationals have chosen as the setting for their videos.

On October 27 and November 3, Prothom Alo visited these areas of Uttara and attempted to speak with local residents and 17 Chinese nationals. The objective was to find out where they were filming and why. However, most of the Chinese nationals were unwilling to speak. Those who showed some interest simply gave their names and nationality before leaving. Some avoided the conversation, saying they did not speak English. They also refused to communicate through Google Translate.

On the afternoon of 27 October, while attempting to speak with one of the people filming in Sector 12 of Uttara, Prothom Alo came across a Bangladeshi woman named Ritu Akhter. She said she worked as a guide for the Chinese nationals and had been working with them for several months. She added that several other Bangladeshi women also assisted the Chinese nationals in a similar capacity.

When asked where the Chinese nationals published the videos they recorded for hours on end, Ritu Akhter called over a Chinese national named Fangyou. After speaking to him in Chinese, she managed to explain that the reporter wanted to talk to him. The conversation then took place through Google Translate on Fangyou's mobile phone.

Fangyou told Prothom Alo that they livestreamed on a Chinese platform called WeChat as part of product promotion activities. However, when asked why they had chosen this particular area of Uttara and why they livestreamed continuously, he refused to answer any further questions. At one point, he sternly called Ritu over and left the scene.

Ritu Akhter told Prothom Alo that she primarily worked as a guide for the Chinese nationals, earning Tk 700 to Tk 800 a day in return. She said the Chinese nationals earned money by posting these videos on China-based platforms such as WeChat and Douyin (TikTok), as well as on various other platforms.

According to Ritu, the Chinese nationals have a particular interest in areas inhabited by low-income people in Bangladesh, which is why they chose this neighbourhood.

How are the videos presented?

The Chinese nationals speak while recording their livestreams. Since they speak Chinese, local residents cannot understand what they are saying. However, it is easy to tell from watching that they are describing the subjects they are livestreaming.

Some of their commentary during livestreams was translated using Google Translate and verified by four Bangladeshis who know Chinese. An analysis of the content revealed that although the videos are being recorded in Uttara, the Chinese nationals claim during their livestreams that they are broadcasting from New Delhi, India.

Some also describe Bangladeshis as poor people living in dirty and damp conditions. Others claim that Bangladeshi men misuse money whenever they get their hands on some. Meanwhile, some Chinese women who livestream can be heard saying that they live here with their husbands and families because they got married in India.

Although local residents have objected to the activities of the Chinese nationals, the police do not monitor their operations. Police at the local station say they have seen Chinese nationals making such videos in various parts of Uttara but do not know why they are filming

On 1 November, a Chinese woman named Mianmian was standing beside the canal in Sector 12 of Uttara, showing viewers videos of Tekpara. She introduced herself as being from China's Sichuan province. During her livestream, she said, “This is New Delhi. Their homes are extremely dirty. There isn't even a fan inside the tin-roofed houses. This place is quite underdeveloped, dirty and unhygienic, and the law-and-order situation is poor.”

She went on to describe how people in India use toilets.

There are tea stalls on both sides of a small bridge in Tekpara. Another Chinese national, named Wang Wei, was filming at these tea stalls. During his livestream, he could be heard saying, “Look, they are drinking tea. Do you know what kind of tea this is? This is cow urine tea. They drink cow urine tea.”

Standing in front of another tea stall, he claimed during his livestream that the tea people were drinking was made using dirty river water. He also described their lifestyle as extremely unhygienic.

However, some of the Chinese nationals were also heard making positive comments about Bangladesh.

A Chinese national named Li Yang, while showing air conditioners installed in various buildings in Uttara, said, “Look, they use air conditioners too. Most of these air conditioners are Chinese. Everyone uses Chinese products because they think they are cheap here. Can you tell me which brand this air conditioner is? Whoever can guess correctly will receive a prize.”

Privacy concerns raised

Chinese nationals have been filming in almost every alley and street of Uttara for months. They sometimes record videos several times in the same area on a single day. They film not only on roads and in shops but also enter residential neighbourhoods to record videos. Local residents complain that these Chinese nationals sometimes walk into people's homes while filming.

Rozina Khatun, a local resident, told Prothom Alo, “Sometimes they enter our homes and start filming. We are not always properly dressed inside our houses. Imagine how it feels when someone suddenly walks into your home and starts recording.”

Another resident, Papia Begum, said, “Some of them even enter bathrooms while filming. Even if we say something to them, they don't understand. They just smile, say sorry and leave. This kind of nuisance continues throughout the day. Nobody takes any action either. If we confront them, they leave, but then come back again.”

No monitoring or oversight

Although local residents have objected to the activities of the Chinese nationals, the police do not monitor their operations. Police at the local station say they have seen Chinese nationals making such videos in various parts of Uttara but do not know why they are filming. They say that attempts to find out more have been hampered by language barriers and the Chinese nationals' apparent irritation, leading them to avoid pursuing the matter.

Mohammad Khalid Mansur, officer-in-charge (OC) of Uttara West Police Station, told Prothom Alo, “I actually don't know why they make these videos. I don't know where the videos are screened either. However, I have informed senior authorities that they are making these videos. Work is underway on the matter.”

item.title: Politics of fear failed to stop El-Sayed's historic US Senate win
item.description:
USA-ELECTION/MICHIGAN

The US president repeatedly branded him a jihadist. His Republican opponent questioned his loyalty to America. Campaign mailers suggested he had ties to terrorists and warned that, if elected, he would bring sharia law to Michigan.

Before Abdul El-Sayed could make history as the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, he endured what critics called one of the most overtly Islamophobic campaigns in modern US politics.

He won anyway. El-Sayed cast his victory in Tuesday's midterm elections as a rebuke to such rhetoric, accusing his Republican opponent Mike Rogers of running what he called a historically ugly, hate-based campaign.

"You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," El-Sayed said in his victory speech.

The attacks were a defining feature of the race, stirring safety concerns among residents in and around Dearborn, home to one of the nation's largest Arab American communities, local officials and residents said this week.

El-Sayed, 42, a Michigan-born Egyptian American who has a medical degree and formerly served as Detroit's health director, ran as a progressive focused on healthcare and the cost of living.

David Kolar, a 32-year-old music teacher, said the focus on El-Sayed's faith recalled the backlash Muslims faced after the 11 September 2001 attacks, a period he believed the country had left behind.

"We have freedom of religion, and if he is of the Muslim faith, so be it," Kolar said after casting his ballot for El-Sayed in the Detroit suburb of Warren.

US Midterm Elections: A ‘regime change’ in the US without bloodshed

Rogers said his objections to El-Sayed were ideological, not religious. Yet he portrayed him as a national security threat and campaigned alongside Republicans who went further.

Foremost among them was President Donald Trump, who labeled El-Sayed a terrorist and compared him to the 11 September hijackers. Rogers appeared with Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican who said El-Sayed sleeps "in a bin Laden jersey," and with Senator Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican, when he called El-Sayed a "jihadist leprechaun" and warned Americans would die if he won.

The attacks stood out not only for their severity but for how readily prominent Republicans embraced them, said Nazita Lajevardi, an associate professor at the University of Michigan who studies the intersection of politics, race and religion.

Unlike after September 11 or during Trump's first-term Muslim ban, she said, there was little pushback from Republican party elites.

"This is the most egregious and most bigoted Islamophobic campaign I have seen," she said. "What you’re seeing is not just hostility, racism and bigotry from the president ... but you're seeing it from rank-and-file members of the Republican Party."

Anatomy of an attack campaign

Led by Trump, Republicans portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist throughout the campaign. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was derided in Texas as "Talafreako" over his views on gender and sexuality. In Ohio, ads weaponized Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's account of surviving sexual assault in her youth.

Voters appeared far more concerned with pocketbook issues than attacks, however, in an election season when Democrats, including Talarico and Acton, chalked up sweeping wins.

Still, perhaps no campaign leaned into identity politics as heavily as the Michigan Senate race.

Republicans sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood using decade-old writings on political change in Egypt and social media posts by his half-sister. The United States designated some Brotherhood branches as terrorist organizations this year. El-Sayed disavowed the group and denied any association, and no evidence has emerged linking him to it.

Republicans also seized on El-Sayed's response to the March attack on Michigan's Temple Israel synagogue. In a statement denouncing the violence, he said "hurt people hurt people," drawing anger from some Jewish leaders who criticized the remark as rationalizing antisemitic violence.

Trump’s midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data centre opponents

He later apologised, saying that his comments may have been misconstrued and that "it wasn't the time for context."

Rogers' allies invoked the episode through the campaign's final hours. On the eve of the election, the Michigan Republican Party held a press conference featuring Jewish and Black community leaders opposed to El-Sayed beside a large red sign accusing him of offering "SAFE HARBOR TO TERRORISTS."

Asked by Reuters to substantiate the claim, party communications director Ted Goodman pointed to the "hurt people hurt people" remark, which he said amounted to justifying a terrorist attack against children.

The argument resonated with some voters. Five of roughly 30 people Reuters interviewed in the Detroit area said El-Sayed's Muslim faith or perceived links to extremism strongly influenced their vote for Rogers.

Robin Cook, 73, was one of them. "I don't think he's a true American," he said of El-Sayed. "I don't trust him."

Dearborn pushes back

Most voters interviewed dismissed the attacks as desperate and a distraction from their economic concerns. Non-Muslims stressed that Muslims and Arab Americans were woven into their daily lives, pointing to friends, neighbors, colleagues and physicians in their communities.

"I grew up around all nationalities," said Pamela Johnson, a 72-year-old Catholic, after voting for El-Sayed. "We all matter, regardless of color, race or whatever."

But Dearborn residents said the rhetoric carried real-world consequences, fueling safety fears.

Imad Soofi, a business owner who immigrated from Yemen two decades ago, said he had seen a rise in anti-Muslim hostility since Trump began targeting El-Sayed, including remarks directed at women wearing hijabs in public.

A three-time Trump voter, Soofi, 49, said he might have backed Rogers had the candidate distanced himself from Trump's anti-Muslim rhetoric. Instead, he voted for El-Sayed.

Alabas Farhat, who represents parts of Dearborn and Detroit in the Michigan House, said the campaign recycled anti-Muslim tropes Arab Americans in the region had encountered for years.

"There has been this constant questioning of how American can you be as a Muslim? How American can you be as an Arab American?" Farhat said in an interview. "It happens, but time and again, we show how American we are."

item.title: "Same old story" says Mahfuj Alam, Tasnim Jara sees long political journey ahead
item.description:
Following Samantha Sharmin's resignation from the National Citizen Party (NCP), Mahfuj Alam and Tasnim Jara have shared posts regarding her on Facebook.

A smear campaign was launched against Samantha Sharmin, alleged Mahfuj Alam, former adviser to the interim government and organiser of the new political platform 'Alternatives’. Meanwhile, physician and young politician Tasnim Jara has spoken highly of her.

Samantha Sharmin resigned from NCP on Thursday afternoon. Later that night, Tasnim Jara published a post praising her on Facebook. Mahfuj Alam also posted about Samantha Sharmin on Friday morning.

NCP was formed out of the National Citizen Committee, where Samantha Sharmin served as a spokesperson.

Referring to this background, Mahfuj Alam wrote in his Facebook post that those who played a key role in the transformation and expansion of the six-member Anti-Discrimination Student Movement Liaison Committee into the National Citizens’ Committee, which had more than 400 members, are now being subjected to smear campaigns and malicious propaganda.

He noted that many such incidents had occurred before, adding that the party's leadership at the time had established this precedent from the day the party was founded. The same thing happened to Samantha Sharmin on Thursday, he added.

In his post, Mahfuj Alam said the party would not have been formed so quickly without the people who played key roles in the Liaison Committee and the National Citizens’ Committee. He wrote, "So, be grateful to those who laid the foundation but left because of the alliance. They worked day and night and that is why you found the party in a certain shape. If you cannot show gratitude, at least remain silent for the sake of political coexistence and healthy practices."

In her Facebook post, Tasnim Jara praised Samantha Sharmin warmly. She wrote that there is no shortage of people who want to speak in politics but very few come to listen. Samantha was one of those few people.

She works tirelessly, yet whenever someone approaches her to speak, she stops and listens fully. She never lets anyone feel that she is in a rush. She reaches out to people to understand their lives and to stand beside them.

Tasnim Jara added, "Her political journey still has a long way to go. Our politics needs more people like her and they deserve a much bigger place in it."

Samantha Sharmin was among the founding leaders of NCP. When the young people who led the July mass uprising formed the party nearly two years ago, she became its senior convener.

A former student of Dhaka University, Samantha Sharmin most recently served as a joint convener of NCP. She left the party two weeks after being demoted in its reconstituted committee.

Explaining her decision to leave, Samantha Sharmin said the NCP is being swallowed up by Jamaat-e-Islami because it lacks a clear political ‘line’ of its own. She said the party of young people who led the mass uprising is now having to play a reactionary and supporting role for Jamaat on various issues.

Samantha also believes that NCP's decision to contest the election as a subordinate appendage of a larger political party has exhausted the possibility of developing its own new political platform. She further said NCP's stance has been aligning with conservative political trends that are hostile to women. Samantha also expressed dissatisfaction with the reconstitution of the NCP committee without holding a council.

item.title: HRW urges police not to use excessive force against protesting garment workers
item.description:
The US-based international human rights organisation Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called on the police in Bangladesh not to use excessive force against garment workers protesting for higher wages. The organisation has also called for those responsible for violence to be held accountable.

HRW made the appeal to the Bangladeshi authorities in a report published yesterday, Thursday. The report is available on HRW’s website.

The report said, Bangladesh police have used batons and tear gas to disperse thousands of garment workers protesting for higher wages. Violence by thugs allegedly linked to factory owners and political parties, arson, factory vandalism, and attacks on police have all been reported.

The HRW said, consistent with international standards, Bangladesh authorities should ensure that police use force only when necessary and proportionate, and that those responsible for violence are held accountable.

A garment worker, Toufiq Hossain, died on 3 November. A co-worker who had been with him told Human Rights Watch: “We were returning to the factory [after lunch] when Toufiq got caught between protesting workers and men hired to tackle the protest by another garment factory. When I looked back, I saw Toufiq lying on the ground. The hired men had beaten him brutally.”

The striking workers are seeking a monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$241), up from the 12,500 taka set in 2023. The government formed a wage board on 1 November, which announced that a new pay structure, once determined, will apply from December.

“My rent is 6,000 taka ($48),” a 31-year-old sewing machine operator said. “Cooking gas now costs 2,300 ($18.50). I earn 13,500 ($108) [a month]. This year I can’t afford my children’s schooling. Tell me, what’s left for food?”

The report also said, instead of addressing legitimate demands for living wages, Bangladeshi authorities are blaming the political opposition for instigating protests. On 3 November, Dhaka police said they had arrested 33 supporters of the former ruling party, the Awami League, for sabotage. Others alleged that members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) youth wing had marched against protesting workers.

Three labour leaders were reportedly detained in Ashulia on November 3, accused of incitement. Police have also filed cases under Anti-Terrorism Act against thousands of unnamed people.

“They took my husband away,” said a 28-year-old woman whose husband was arrested. “He had joined the protest for a short time. He wasn’t involved in any violence.”

The report mentioned, the BNP government promised inflation-linked wages before its election in February. An amendment to the Labour Act, adopted in April, provides for wage reviews every three years and prohibits employers from blacklisting trade union organisers.

HRW said, Bangladesh authorities should end the cycle of violence and impunity around wage negotiations. Global brands also have a role to play; they should always ensure that their contracts with suppliers don’t incentivise workplace abuses or make living wages impracticable.

item.title: Hasan takes 6 wickets as West Indies bowled out for 356
item.description:
Hasan Mahmud claimed six wickets as West Indies were bowled out for 356 in their first innings on the second day of the Sylhet Test on Friday.

Hasan took the final wicket, bowling Shamar Joseph with the first ball of the second session. Joseph tried to move towards the leg side and play a 128kph delivery but was beaten as the ball came in and struck the middle and leg stumps.

It was Hasan’s sixth wicket of the innings and his fifth five-wicket haul in Test cricket. It was also his first five-wicket haul on home soil. He became the first Bangladesh fast bowler to take a wicket by stumping in Test cricket. He also joined Nathan Lyon as the only bowlers to claim their first five-wicket hauls in five different countries.

Hasan had taken three wickets in the morning session, including two in successive deliveries with the second new ball. He dismissed centurion Aamir Jangoo, who was bowled, and West Indies captain Roston Chase, who was caught behind.

Hasan then had a chance to complete a hat-trick, but Joshua Bishop survived after a review showed the ball had taken an inside edge before hitting his pad.

Hasan later dismissed Bishop to complete his five-wicket haul. His other wickets were Kavem Hodge and Kevin Wickham. He had previously taken five wickets against Afghanistan last October.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz also claimed a wicket in the morning session, dismissing Justin Greaves for 51. Greaves was beaten by a delivery that went straight on and hit his off stump.

West Indies added 87 runs and lost four wickets in the first session of the day. They went to lunch at 322 for 8, with Hasan having taken five wickets. Miraz had another chance to add to his tally when he trapped Joseph leg before wicket with the last ball before lunch, but Joseph survived after a review.

Earlier in the day, Bangladesh suffered an injury setback when opener Shadman Islam twisted his left ankle while trying to stop a boundary. His ankle became caught up in the grass and twisted, leaving him in considerable pain. He was eventually carried off the field on a stretcher.

At the end of the innings, Hasan finished with six wickets, while Taskin Ahmed took two and Miraz one.

Brief score

West Indies 1st innings: 356 all out in 106.3 overs (Jangoo 133, Wickham 61, Greaves 51, Bishop 23, Joseph 16*, Warrican 27*, Seales 15; Hasan 6/90, Taskin 2/90, Miraz 2/82, Taijul 0/54, Nayeem 0/37).

item.title: Dhaka University still requires students to visit bank to pay Tk 1 fine
item.description:
The fine is just Tk 1. Yet a Dhaka University student has to go to a bank and stand in a queue to pay it. This is what happens when students return library books eight or nine days late.

In an age of technology-driven services, the requirement to visit a bank to pay a fine of just Tk 1 may seem astonishing to many. Yet this system has been in place for years at Dhaka University’s Central Library and the Science Library under its supervision. Although many other university services are now available online, the method of paying library fines has remained unchanged.

The issue has come under renewed discussion following a social media post by a Dhaka University student. Nabila Haque, a student of the Department of Physics in the 2023-24 academic session, wrote about it on her Facebook account on Thursday.

In an age of technology-driven services, the requirement to visit a bank to pay a fine of just Tk 1 may seem astonishing to many. Yet this system has been in place for years at Dhaka University’s Central Library and the Science Library under its supervision.

Nabila Haque was fined Tk 1 by the university’s Science Library for returning a book eight or nine days late. She has to deposit the money at the Janata Bank branch in the university’s Teacher-Student Centre (TSC).

University sources say the Science Library operates under Dhaka University’s Central Library. However, the libraries of the university’s various halls and departments follow their own rules.

The student’s post includes a photograph of a library fine collection form. Alongside her name, department, hall and library card details, the amount of the fine is listed as “Tk 1”. The form bears the signature of a library official dated 3 November.

One-taka paper notes are now rarely seen in everyday transactions. On 29 May 2025, Bangladesh Bank announced the introduction of newly designed banknotes, but the list did not include a one-taka note. However, one-taka coins remain in circulation.

Student questions the hassle over Tk 1

Prothom Alo spoke to the student who was fined. She said the book’s return deadline fell during the Puja holidays, so she could not return it on time. In her words, “Having to go to the bank over just one taka is frustrating.”

Mohammad Mostakim, a student of Shahid Sergeant Zahurul Haque Hall who regularly studies at the university’s Central Library, told Prothom Alo, “The university could bring this fine payment process under its online services. Having to go all the way to the bank and stand in a queue to pay a fine of just one taka is a form of harassment for students.”

Mostakim said many university services could now be accessed online. If students were allowed to pay fines online as well, it would save them both time and trouble.

Prothom Alo spoke to the student who was fined. She said the book’s return deadline fell during the Puja holidays, so she could not return it on time. In her words, “Having to go to the bank over just one taka is frustrating.”

Two different fine rates on the website

Dhaka University’s Central Library website lists two different rates for fines on late book returns.

The ‘Fine Details’ section of the website states that students are fined 50 paisa for delays during the first and second weeks, Tk 1 during the third and fourth weeks, and Tk 3 from the fifth week onwards. However, it is not clear whether these amounts apply to each week or represent the total fine for the specified periods.

On the other hand, Rule 14 of the library’s ordinance-based regulations, also published on the same website, stipulates a fine of 25 paisa per book for each week or part of a week that a student is late in returning it. According to that rule, the fine is supposed to be collected in cash at the university’s Accounts Office. Yet students currently have to go to a bank to pay the fine.

In other words, there are discrepancies between the fine rates and collection procedures stated in the ordinance-based regulations and those listed elsewhere on the university website. The website provides no explanation as to whether these rules have been changed since publication or which rules are currently in effect.

Other fees can be paid online, but not a one-taka fine

The requirement to visit a bank to pay a fine of just Tk 1 raises further questions in light of the university’s own initiatives.

In a notice issued on 13 May 2025, Dhaka University’s Public Relations Office announced that, starting from the 2024-25 academic session, first-year students would be able to pay various fees, including departmental, institute and hall deposits, either online or at the relevant offices.

The university authorities said the initiative had been taken to reduce students’ difficulties. As a result, they would no longer have to stand in long queues at banks as they had in the past.

In other words, while the university has introduced a system in some areas to spare students the inconvenience of standing in bank queues, the Central Library of the same university still leaves a bank as the only option for paying a fine of just Tk 1.

Thousands of students use Dhaka University’s Central Library. It is reasonable to have deadlines for returning books and rules for imposing fines. But when the fine amounts to just Tk 1, questions arise over the rationale for making students visit a bank and go through a formal payment process.

‘A 40- to 50-year-old rule, it is illogical’

Professor Kazi Mostak Gausul Hoq, acting librarian of Dhaka University’s Central Library, considers the requirement to visit a bank to pay a one-taka fine illogical.

He told Prothom Alo that collecting a one-taka fine through a bank was unreasonable. The system had been in place for a long time—around 40 to 50 years, or even longer.

The librarian said that bank payment was currently the only way to deposit fines. However, he would discuss with the higher authorities whether an alternative arrangement could be introduced for paying small amounts.

The fine payment process is also a form of ‘punishment’

Dhaka University Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Administration) Professor Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane, however, believes the process of paying fines is also intended to make students more careful.

He told Prothom Alo that all financial transactions at Dhaka University are conducted through banks, which is why fines for late book returns also have to be paid there. The process students have to go through to pay even a small fine serves as a form of punishment. It also reminds them not to deliberately delay returning books in the future.

However, the pro-vice-chancellor said the university would take steps to change the old system. He said initiatives would be taken to bring these services online. The university administration would also work on allowing students to pay fines using QR codes.

item.title: US Midterm Elections: A ‘regime change’ in the US without bloodshed
item.description:
President Donald Trump kept pounding away at Iran with the aim of toppling its government. Thousands of civilians were killed in the bombings. Around 10,000 important installations were destroyed. He even threatened to use a deadly weapon he described as the “mother of all bombs”. Yet, eight months later, Iran’s government remains firmly in power.

Last Tuesday, however, American voters brought about a kind of “regime change” in their own country without dropping a single bomb or firing a single bullet. They did not remove Trump from the presidency, but they took away his party’s control of both chambers of Congress, putting a check on his absolute power.

Trump himself had told his supporters to assume that his name was on the ballot, even though it was not. The voters seem to have taken him at his word, delivering a verdict against Trump and Trumpism. In the words of many, this was not merely a blue or Democratic wave; it was a veritable tsunami.

Last Tuesday, however, American voters brought about a kind of “regime change” in their own country without dropping a single bomb or firing a single bullet. They did not remove Trump from the presidency, but they took away his party’s control of both chambers of Congress, putting a check on his absolute power.
Trump’s midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data centre opponents

A referendum on Trump

Midterm elections in the United States have always served as a referendum on the sitting president and his party’s performance in government. Over the past 100 years, with only three exceptions, incumbent presidents have suffered humiliating defeats at the hands of voters. During Barack Obama’s first term, his party lost 63 seats in the 2010 midterm elections.

The final seat tally in this election is not yet clear. However, according to unofficial results, Democrats have regained control of both chambers of Congress. They have wrested at least seven Senate seats from Republicans. Democrats have also won the governorships of deeply conservative states such as Texas, Georgia and Ohio, ousting Republican incumbents. Trump had won Texas by a double-digit margin just two years ago. The result there this time shows just how far the Democratic wave has swept.

Trump and his Republican administration had made extensive preparations to retain power. Electoral maps were redrawn in violation of established rules. The Department of Justice was instructed to investigate alleged election fraud.

Orders were issued to revise voter rolls over allegations that undocumented immigrants had been included on them. More than 1,000 federal election monitors were deployed.

Party supporters were told to guard polling stations to prevent fraud. There were even reports of plans to declare a “state of emergency” if none of these measures worked. But nothing helped. The reason was that Americans were no longer willing to tolerate the corruption, misconduct and abuse of power by this administration.

The main reason: The economy

In 1992, James Carville, a strategist for Bill Clinton’s election campaign, summed up the central message of the campaign in one line: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democrats kept that old lesson in mind during this year’s midterm elections. The cost of living was at the centre of their campaign.

Voters judged the state of the economy by their grocery bills and the prices at petrol stations. In an Associated Press voter survey, most respondents said Trump’s policies had increased their expenses.

The war with Iran has driven up energy prices, which means higher prices for almost all goods. After the election, Vice President JD Vance said, “The reason we lost is the war.” His admission is particularly significant. The decision to enter the war, whose cost voters have had to bear, was made by his own president.

Apart from the war with Iran, another reason for the rising cost of living is the trade war. After taking office, Trump announced sweeping import tariffs without considering the consequences. He said, “We are making trillions of dollars from tariffs.” He failed to understand that the money was actually being taken from ordinary consumers in the form of taxes.

Trump also refused to believe that the cost of living was becoming unaffordable for people. He called it a “hoax” fabricated by the Democrats. Even in the week before the election, he refused to acknowledge that rising fuel prices had created a crisis in the country.

He said, “Prices may have gone up a little, but surely that is a sacrifice worth making to destroy Iran’s nuclear weapons.” At an election rally, he even said, “We have greatly benefited from rising fuel prices.” That was true, but by “we” he meant himself, his family and America’s millionaire class.

Democrats take US Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump

Verdict against hate

The central message of Trump’s “Make America Great Again”, or MAGA, movement has been hatred towards all non-white people, particularly brown people from the developing world.

They are portrayed as outsiders and as threats to America’s Christian and white civilisation. Vice President JD Vance had said that the presence of outsiders had brought the United States to the brink of “civilisational erasure”.

One of the main reasons for Trump’s victory in the 2024 election was his hardline stance against illegal immigration. It must be acknowledged that this tough approach effectively halted the influx of undocumented immigrants across the southern border, earning him praise.

But in the name of stopping illegal immigration, he launched military-style operations across the country, primarily targeting immigrants from South America, particularly Mexico. Immigration officers wearing masks, known as ICE agents, began wreaking havoc in cities across the United States under the pretext of deporting them.

Parents were arrested and taken away in front of their young children. On allegations of illegal entry, people were shackled and sent to a third country. Several American citizens were also killed in ICE shootings.

This anti-immigration campaign was one of the main reasons behind the Republicans’ defeat in the midterm elections. In 2024, Mexican Americans in Texas and Arizona had voted overwhelmingly for Trump. This time, they voted against him.

It was because of the Hispanic vote that Texas elected a Democratic senator for the first time in 40 years. A Hispanic woman also became governor. Republicans lost control of the Texas House of Representatives as well.

One of these so-called outsiders is Michigan’s newly elected senator, Abdul El-Sayed. President Trump described him in various ways—as a jihadist, a terrorist and a threat to the United States.

The aim was to instil hatred in the minds of Michigan voters towards him and other people considered outsiders. El-Sayed has been a vocal critic of Israel over the genocide in Gaza. As a result, tens of millions of dollars were spent trying to stop him.

Voters were told that if elected, he would not be allowed anywhere near the US Senate. And even if he managed to get there, he would have to pass through the metal detectors installed to prevent terrorism before entering the Senate.

El-Sayed’s achievement was that he did not take the bait thrown out by Trump and the Republicans. He said his goal was to stop money from controlling politics and put it back in people’s pockets, while ensuring healthcare for everyone. After winning the election, El-Sayed addressed JD Vance, who had called him a fraud, saying, “Habibi, now you are obliged to swear me in as a senator. That is your constitutional duty.”

Trump blames Democrats winning midterms for US stocks fall

What the transfer of power means

Under the US Constitution, all powers of the state are divided equally among the executive, legislature and judiciary. President Trump has not respected this distribution of power. In an interview with The New York Times, he said that no law applied to him and that he could do whatever he wanted. He said, “The only thing that can stop me is my own morality.” His loyal Republicans never dared to stand in his way in Congress. In most cases, even the Supreme Court gave him a free pass.

That situation will now change. Trump will have to turn to Congress to pass any new legislation or secure budget approval and funding. With their substantial majority, the incoming Congress will have the power to hold the Trump administration accountable on every front—from the war and trade policy to immigration and judicial investigations.

The question is whether Democrats will spend all their time using that power to investigate the Trump administration. Hakeem Jeffries has made it clear that their priority will not be investigations but finding ways to make life more affordable for people. That is the message they have taken from this election.

A major defeat for Elon Musk

Trump and the Republicans suffered a major defeat in the midterm elections. Elon Musk was among those who lost alongside them. The world’s richest man had warned that the United States would be ruined if Democrats won the election. To prevent such an outcome, he spent nearly USD 500 million of his own money. It was all in vain.

One of the key items on the Democrats’ election agenda was to oppose the construction of data centres for artificial intelligence without the consent of local residents. The largest number of data centres are being built in Texas, where Democrats now control every centre of power.

A disappointed Elon Musk lamented, “I guess I’ll have to go to Mars to build data centres.”
