item.title: Shadow cabinet in Bangladesh: Why the opposition must move beyond a paper lineup
item.description:
Introducing a shadow cabinet to a nation that hasn't seen the practice since its post-1990 democratic transition is a welcome departure. Yet, rendering this institution functional and meaningful remains a distinct challenge. It is not an end in itself, nor can it survive as a goal-free pursuit.
Following the 13th parliamentary general election -- where the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won a landslide victory and the Jamaat-led alliance became the main opposition -- Jamaat explicitly announced its willingness to establish a shadow cabinet on February 17, the very day its lawmakers took their oaths.
True to its commitment, the Jamaat-led alliance formally declared a shadow cabinet in late August this year, with the party head designated as the shadow premier.
Yet, what we have witnessed over the subsequent two months is not encouraging for a functioning shadow cabinet.
I would be glad to be proven wrong, but very few people in this nation of 170 million know who sits in this shadow cabinet or who holds which portfolio.
There has been little effort to introduce these shadow ministers to ordinary citizens. Neither has there been much activity to give the public confidence that the shadow cabinet is establishing checks and balances in our parliamentary system.
When a government enters its ninth month in office, it naturally falters on certain promises and deliverables, earning public criticism. This is normal in a democracy.
However, the shadow cabinet remains invisible and unfelt when it comes to political and intellectual engagement -- failing to confront governmental shortcomings or offer superior policy alternatives and governance directions.
For Bangladesh’s formidable opposition, merely announcing a shadow cabinet lineup is not enough. If they mean business, they must introduce their shadow ministers to the public and make these "ministers-in-waiting" familiar faces through their work.
This work must include providing critical analyses of government operations, scrutinizing policies pursued by different ministries and agencies, and publishing policy papers with better alternatives.
Otherwise, a "paper shadow cabinet" will end up being no better than having no shadow cabinet at all.
A shadow cabinet does not just oppose; it proposes. By presenting viable alternative budgets and administrative strategies, it elevates public discourse and gives citizens a clear picture of how an alternative government would rule.
Rather than offering generalized, vague criticisms, assigned shadow ministers must deeply analyze specific portfolios such as home affairs, foreign affairs, health, education, and finance.
Such an exercise would elevate the efficiency of lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, turning parliament into a venue for lively debate.
Burdened by a history of house-boycott culture, Bangladeshi voters have long yearned for a vibrant parliament where policies are vigorously debated to serve the people best.
In a functional system, a shadow cabinet is a team of senior spokespeople chosen by the leader of the opposition to mirror the official cabinet. Each member is appointed to lead a specific policy area for their party, questioning and challenging their counterpart in the government.
In this way, the official opposition presents itself as a credible government-in-waiting. Shadow ministers must directly question, challenge, and monitor the performance, policies, and spending of their government counterparts.
If Bangladesh’s current parliamentary opposition wants to translate its shadow cabinet initiative into meaningful action, it must formulate alternative manifestos and detailed policy proposals to show the electorate how it would govern differently.
Shadow ministers need to lead opposition responses during major legislative debates, push back against government bills in the division lobbies, and use parliamentary questions to pressure sitting ministers.
They must make the best use of parliamentary sessions, choosing strategic topics for debate and bringing forward motions to challenge the government.
Ideally, shadow cabinet members should act as the primary public spokespeople on television, radio, and in the press to critique government actions. This does not happen automatically. It requires a deliberate political process of grooming these designated members so they can outmaneuver government functionaries in public and press debates.
Politics in Bangladesh is historically adversarial and deeply polarized. The relationship between the ruling party and the opposition is often treated as a winner-take-all battle, leaving little room for the mutual recognition and institutional cooperation that a shadow cabinet demands.
Yet, in a parliamentary democracy, seats on both the treasury and opposition benches are inherently temporary. The party in power today may well find itself on the opposition benches tomorrow.
What must remain permanent is a commitment to robust institutional practices -- and a shadow cabinet system should be at the very heart of that foundation.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: 88 garment factories resume operations in Ashulia
item.description:
A total of 88 garment factories remained open in the Ashulia industrial zone of Savar, Dhaka, on Friday, while the overall situation remained peaceful and normal.
Industrial police personnel were deployed at different locations as a precautionary measure.
The situation was observed during visits to Hemayetpur, Savar and different parts of Ashulia from Friday morning.
Industrial police said some factories normally operate on weekly holidays, particularly those facing urgent shipment deadlines. Workers joined their shifts peacefully at all 88 factories from the morning, with no reports of disorder.
Additional Superintendent of Police of Industrial Police-1 Shoaib Ahmed said factories generally remain closed on Fridays, but those with urgent operational requirements keep running.
Superintendent of Police of Industrial Police-1 Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan said police personnel were performing their regular duties across the industrial zone.
Khairul Mamun Mintu, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, said some factories normally operate on weekly holidays to meet urgent requirements.
He said they had already urged workers to return to work peacefully and that the industrial zone had maintained a peaceful environment since Thursday.
“We expect the situation to remain peaceful as factories resume full-scale operations,” he said.
Mintu said a wage board had been formed and workers' demands and grievances over wages should now be addressed through discussions.
He said workers should return to their workplaces and keep production running while awaiting the wage board's decision.
However, he warned that fear among workers could make their return difficult.
He called for an end to alleged police searches and harassment at workers' homes, stressing the need to ensure their safety and a normal working environment.

item.title: Trump blames Democrats winning midterms for US stocks fall
item.description:
US President Donald Trump attributed Thursday's stock market freefall to the electoral victory of his rival Democratic Party in midterm elections earlier this week.
"The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday - So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" Trump posted on his Truth Social platform after US markets closed for the day.
Analysts attributed Thursday's stock selloff to fears of Democrats threatening the AI data center investment boom, with the tech-focused Nasdaq suffering its worst session percentage-wise since April 2025.
Data centers have faced broad opposition from US voters regardless of political affiliation, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.

item.title: Applied Human Science College students demand principal's resignation
item.description:
Students of Government College of Applied Human Science, formerly known as Home Economics College, staged a sit-in for a second consecutive day on Friday, blocking the road in front of the institution in Dhaka's Azimpur and demanding the principal's resignation and an investigation into alleged police assaults on students.
They issued a 72-hour ultimatum for the fulfilment of their two-point demands, warning that they would continue their movement until the demands were met.
The protest began at 8am on Friday, with students chanting slogans including “Home Economics has risen”, “Why were police on campus? We want answers” and “Why was my sister injured? We want answers”.
Their first demand is the resignation of Principal Professor Meherunnessa. They said classes and examinations would remain suspended and the principal would not be allowed on campus until she submits a written resignation.
Their second demand is an investigation into the police operation at the college and its residential halls late on Wednesday night, including allegations of baton charges and assaults on students. They also demanded an update on the investigation within 72 hours and punishment for those responsible.
The protest began on Thursday morning, when students gathered outside the principal's office at around 10:30am and later locked her inside by putting a padlock on the office door.
Police arrived at around 11:30pm and rescued the principal after nearly 13 hours. However, more than 100 students continued their demonstration outside the college until around 2:30am.
Students alleged that police dragged female students down the stairs by their hair, beat them and charged at them with batons during the operation.
Several students were injured, according to the protesters, with three to four receiving hospital treatment. One student, who was allegedly trampled by police, is being treated at Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
The protesters also alleged that police entered the residential halls and assaulted students. They further claimed that officers took away several students' mobile phones and identity cards.
The students said the movement was not politically motivated but stemmed from their opposition to the principal's alleged arbitrary decisions and misconduct towards students. They said several of their classmates had been injured, with some still receiving treatment at hospitals.
Although the students had resume their sit-in at 8am on Friday, they said they would allow scheduled recruitment examinations to take place. However, they demanded that the principal be barred from entering the campus during the examinations.
The dispute began over a farewell program held at the college auditorium before the Puja holidays.
According to students and college administration sources, postgraduate final-year students from five departments across three residential halls were initially allowed to hold the program until 10pm. Following their request, the deadline was extended to midnight, but the event continued until 5am.
Principal Meherunnessa subsequently decided to cancel the residential hall seats of two students who coordinated the program, citing the use of the auditorium beyond the permitted time.
Students alleged that when the two approached her to apologise, she demanded Tk12,600 to cover the auditorium's air-conditioning and electricity costs for the night as a condition for reinstating their residential seats.
The principal, however, denied the allegations.
Speaking to journalists on Thursday evening, Meherunnessa said the students had been permitted to hold the programme until midnight but continued until 5am.
She said she initially cancelled the residential seats of the two students over the violation but later softened her position after they apologised. However, she decided to recover the cost of electricity wastage to maintain discipline.
“What the students are saying is the total opposite of what happened. I allowed them to hold a programme until midnight. They continued until 5am. I became a little angry and cancelled the residential seats of the two students,” she said.
Responding to the demand for her resignation, she said: “They are asking me to sign my resignation on a blank sheet of paper. Why should I resign to them?”
Lalbagh police station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Jamil Hossain said students were staging a sit-in demanding the principal's resignation.
“The situation is calm. Police are present at the scene,” he said.

item.title: Kumarkhali loses Tk 35C in potential farm output annually to waterlogging
item.description:
Around 1,250 hectares of cultivable land in Kumarkhali upazila of Kushtia remain waterlogged for seven to eight months every year, causing an estimated annual loss of Tk35 crore in potential agricultural production.
The upazila, surrounded by the Padma, Gorai, Kaliganga and Dakua rivers, has around 18,240 hectares of cultivable land. Farmers can grow crops on the waterlogged land only once a year during the Boro season, producing around 6,225 tonnes of paddy.
If the waterlogging problem is resolved, the land could produce an additional 10,000 tonnes of paddy and other crops during the Aman and Aus seasons, with an estimated market value of Tk35 crore.
Agricultural officials and local farmers say food production could increase further if modern farming methods and high-yielding crop varieties were introduced.
Farmers said although the upazila had numerous irrigation canals under the Ganges-Kobadak (G-K) Irrigation Project, managed by the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), there was no proper drainage system.
Many canals have remained neglected for years, while some have been filled in to build houses and others blocked by dams for fish farming.
As a result, land that could produce crops three times a year remains submerged for seven to eight months, severely affecting agriculture.
Farmers said the problem continued for nearly a decade without any effective initiative to resolve it. This has reduced agricultural production and caused recurring financial losses for farmers.
A visit to the wetlands of Bahalbaria, Chandpur, Banshara, Bakhai, Karatkandi and Jagonnathpur found large areas under water. Stagnant water was covered with water hyacinths, water spinach (kolmi) and water lilies. Some locals were seen fishing from small boats, while others cleared weeds to prepare their land for cultivation this season.
Many farmers have turned to fish farming by digging ponds after suffering repeated losses from crop cultivation. Ponds have also been dug along canals near the wetlands, while houses and roads have been built in the areas.
Poor maintenance has also left many canals unable to drain water properly.
Rabiul Islam, a farmer from Bahalbaria Beel in Nandolalpur union, said he owned 16 bighas of land.
"Ten to 12 years ago, water used to flow through a canal into the Gorai River, allowing us to grow rice three times a year. Now, as water cannot drain out, we can barely grow even one crop," he said.
Majed Ali, another farmer from the same area, said it was frustrating that water remained stagnant despite the presence of four nearby rivers.
"The stagnant water is covered with water hyacinths and weeds. Clearing them requires six labourers per bigha. Farming has become costly, but yields and profits remain low," he said.
Abdus Samad, a farmer from the Gobindapur Beel area, said some areas had no canals, while existing ones were clogged with weeds and silt.
As a result, water remains trapped on the land, allowing farmers to cultivate crops only once a year.
He said planned excavation of canals could help farmers grow crops three times a year.
Azahar Biswas, a farmer aged over 60, owns three bighas of land in Karatkandi Beel under Sadki union.
He said farmers were struggling because of the lack of proper drainage channels.
A single harvest produces around 12 to 14 maunds of rice per bigha, but the income is almost entirely spent on clearing weeds, Azahar said.
"If we could cultivate the land two or three times a year, farming would become profitable," he added.
According to the local Department of Agricultural Extension office, around 1,250 hectares of the upazila's 18,240 hectares of cultivable land are currently waterlogged.
Of the affected land, 290 hectares are in Nandolalpur union, 250 in Sadki, 240 in Jagannathpur, 205 in Shelaidaha, 75 in Jadu Boyra, 120 in Kaya and 70 hectares in Chapra union.
The waterlogging is affecting agricultural production and making it difficult to meet the upazila's overall food production targets.
In 2024, the area of waterlogged land was only 510 hectares, according to the office.
Upazila Agriculture Officer Md Monir Hossain said the extent of waterlogging had increased over the years with rising rainfall.
He said around 1,250 hectares of land were currently affected, producing only 6,225 tonnes of paddy during the Boro season.
If the land could also be cultivated during the Aman and Aus seasons, farmers could have produced an additional 10,000 tonnes of crops, worth around Tk35 crore, the official said.
He added that the issue had been brought to the attention of the local administration and higher authorities.
Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md Raisul Islam said proposals for excavating two canals in Kumarkhali had been submitted under the government's ongoing canal excavation project.
Once the excavation work begins, the waterlogging problem will be partly reduced, he said.
Further initiatives would be taken after discussions with local public representatives, the DAE, farmers, the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) and the BWDB, the UNO said.

item.title: Putin slams 'political' moves to keep Russia out of sport events
item.description:
Vladimir Putin on Thursday slammed countries who oppose reinstating Russia into international sports as several European teams said they will refuse to play them at next year's world ice hockey championships over the Ukraine war.
Denmark, Norway, Sweden and the Czech Republic on Tuesday all followed Finland in saying they would not play Russia at the 2027 world championships to be held in Germany.
Russia has been banned from International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) events since Putin launched the 2022 war in Ukraine, but the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled in favour of admitting them to the world championships.
Russia has been mostly banned from international sport since 2022 but some restrictions have eased in recent months -- a trend slammed by Ukraine.
Putin praised the International Olympic Committee and CAS for "taking decisions to uphold the Olympic Charter and its principles", as restrictions have been eased.
"Unfortunately, however, not all countries are prepared to honour the commitments they once undertook, and restrictions on Russian sport -- which are political rather than legal -- continue," Putin told a televised government meeting.
Amid the ice hockey stand-off, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday Russia would not be allowed to compete at next month's World Junior Hockey Championships.
The world championships are due to be held in Germany next May, but the draw and scheduling for the tournament have already taken place, without Russia.
Putin has regularly appeared playing ice hockey during his long presidency.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands, forced millions to displace and is Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

item.title: Six dead, several hurt in New York house fire
item.description:
Six people died in a house fire on Thursday in New York, authorities said, with Mayor Zohran Mamdani describing the blaze at a Brooklyn home as "devastating."
"I am heartbroken to announce that six New Yorkers lost their lives," Mamdani told reporters, noting that firefighters had responded in under four minutes.
Video from the scene showed orange flames roaring out of several windows at the row-style property in the Sunset Park neighborhood, around five miles (eight kilometres) from Manhattan.
"Four were dead upon FDNY's arrival, while two more passed away at the hospital," Mamdani added, referring to the city's fire department. "All six were adults"
He said four civilians were also hurt, while three firefighters and two police officers suffered minor injuries.
Mamdani added that it was still too early to determine the cause of the fire, but the results of an investigation would be made public.
"This was a devastating fire. It will take a long time for this neighborhood to mourn the neighbors they lost this morning, and to recover from this immense grief," he said.
Daniel Flynn, first deputy commissioner of the FDNY, said that fire marshals were on the scene probing the blaze.
"This was a terrible tragedy, and hopefully we'll get a cause for you as soon as possible," he added.
Last month, four people died in the Bronx borough of New York after an electric bike battery caught fire inside an apartment.

item.title: Dhaka air quality ‘very unhealthy’ Friday morning
item.description:
Dhaka's air quality turned ‘very unhealthy’ on Friday morning, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 203 at 8:40am.
With this score, the capital ranked fourth among the world's most polluted cities, according to the AQI scale.
A ‘very unhealthy’ air quality level means everyone, regardless of their health condition, may experience more serious health effects or discomfort from air pollution. Even short-term exposure can affect anyone.
Pakistan's Lahore topped the list with an AQI score of 456, followed by India's Delhi with 251 and Kolkata with 221.
On Thursday, Dhaka ranked fifth among the world's most polluted cities, recording an AQI score of 174 at 10:25am.
According to the AQI scale, readings of 101-150 are considered unhealthy for sensitive groups, while scores of 151-200 indicate unhealthy air quality. Readings of 201-300 are classified as very unhealthy, while scores above 301 are considered hazardous and pose serious health risks.
The AQI measures daily air quality and indicates pollution levels and their potential effects on public health.
In Bangladesh, air quality is assessed based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths worldwide each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: DMP arrests 544, files 62 cases in 24 hours
item.description:
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) arrested 544 people and filed 62 cases during regular anti-crime operations across the capital in the 24 hours until 8am on Friday.
Of the total arrests, 144 were made in Mirpur Division, 59 in Tejgaon, 44 in Motijheel, 95 in Wari, 41 in Ramna, 49 in Uttara, 42 in Lalbagh and 55 in Gulshan Division.
Another 15 people were arrested by the Special Response Unit (SRU) and the Detective Branch (DB), said Akhtar Hossain, deputy commissioner (Media and Public Relations) of the DMP.
During the operations, law enforcers also seized 540 grams of cannabis, 6,258 Yaba pills, 4.2 grams of heroin in four sachets, 37 Pethidine injections, two knives and two cutters.
Further legal action against those arrested is underway, he added.

item.title: Australia recruit Hussey as consultant for Ashes and 2027 World Cup
item.description:
Mike Hussey was Friday appointed a consultant coach to the Australian team for next year's blockbuster Ashes series against England and the 2027 World Cup.
The former Australian batsmen revealed in August that England's new red-ball coach, Stephen Fleming, had informally approached him to be their Test batting mentor.
But the 51-year-old knocked back the audacious offer and has instead committed himself to helping his home nation arrest a batting crisis highlighted by their recent 2-1 Test series defeat in South Africa.
Hussey, known as "Mr Cricket" for his technical expertise, will also provide coaching assistance during this month's home T20 series against England and the subsequent four-Test series against New Zealand.
He will additionally work with Australia during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where cricket is on the agenda, and the T20 World Cup in 2028.
"I am extremely excited about being a part of the team in a more formal and meaningful role in the coming years," said Hussey, who played more than 300 matches for Australia across all formats.
"This team has achieved so much in recent times, to which I hope I can add value to the coaching and playing groups ahead of what will be an exciting and challenging period."
Hussey has extensive experience as a coach, including with both Australia and England.
He was part of England's coaching setup when they won the T20 World Cup in 2022 and was the Chennai Super Kings' long-time batting coach under Fleming in the Indian Premier League. He also led Welsh Fire in this year's Hundred.
"Mike has been a highly valued part of our staff in the past and brings a considerable skill set which is complementary to the coaches and players," said Australian head coach Andrew McDonald.
"Not only is his expertise as a player and coach across multiple formats, competitions, countries invaluable, so are his qualities as a person."

item.title: Sobhana nominated for ICC Player of the Month award again
item.description:
Sobhana Mostary has been shortlisted for the ICC Player of the Month award for the second time this year, alongside two of the world's leading all-rounders for October 2026.
The consistent Bangladesh batter is up against India's Deepti Sharma and Australia's Annabel Sutherland for the monthly honour.
The 24-year-old was previously nominated for the ICC Player of the Month award in January.
Mostary made history in October by registering the highest individual score by a Bangladesh women's player in ODI cricket, smashing a brilliant 118 off 134 deliveries against Australia in Brisbane.
It was an innings of immense quality, with Mostary striking 18 boundaries to help Bangladesh post a competitive 220-6 in their 50 overs against the formidable Australian side.
Although her effort was not enough to guide Bangladesh to victory in the match or the series, Mostary showcased her class by scoring 129 runs at an average of 43 across the three-match series, ensuring the visitors left Australian shores with their heads held high.
The other two nominees also enjoyed impressive months.
India's experienced all-rounder Deepti was in fine form in October, making significant contributions with both bat and ball across two formats against Zimbabwe.
Meanwhile, Australia's Sutherland delivered consistent performances with both bat and ball throughout the month, accumulating runs and wickets in the ODI series against Bangladesh and the T20I series against New Zealand.

item.title: Carrick fights for United job ahead of international break
item.description:
Michael Carrick takes charge of Manchester United for what could be the last time against Aston Villa this weekend as he battles to save his job despite a morale-boosting midweek victory over Roma.
United's dramatic win in the Champions League gave the coach breathing space but he remains under intense pressure ahead of the international break.
Elsewhere in the Premier League, Manchester City will be seeking to avoid a rare third straight league defeat when they face Nottingham Forest as they try to keep pace with leaders Arsenal.
AFP Sport looks at three talking points ahead of the action:
Carrick's last chance?
When Manchester United's players trudged off at half-time against Roma on Tuesday, 2-0 down and seemingly out of ideas, Michael Carrick's fate appeared to be sealed.
Instead, his underperforming team somehow turned things around, with Matheus Cunha scoring two late goals in a 3-2 win at a feverish Old Trafford.
It ended a run of nine games without a victory -- United's longest winless run since the 1988/89 season.
Defender Diogo Dalot said he hopes the Roma result can kickstart their season.
"Nights like this can change momentum, can change seasons, and I think this win is going to give us confidence for the next games," he said.
But the brutal reality is that United could be bottom of the Premier League when they kick off on Sunday if results go against them.
Whatever the outcome, the international break will give the club's hierarchy an opportunity to consider their long-term options.
Villa's Spanish manager, Unai Emery, was tipped as a potential candidate for the Old Trafford hot seat but reports suggest he is close to signing a new deal with the Birmingham club.
Two-way title race?
Manchester City know that even if they keep pace with Mikel Arteta's Arsenal, it might ultimately all be in vain.
The Etihad club are still waiting to discover their fate after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules -- with a huge points deduction one potential punishment.
Arsenal appear to be the only other serious contender for the title, having the happy knack of winning even when below par.
On paper, both clubs face a straightforward task this weekend, though City's trip to Nottingham Forest could be trickier than it looks.
Opta's "expected points" table, which orders the Premier League based on expected goals for and against, has Oliver Glasner's team in third -- a remarkable 16 places higher than they are in the real table.
Arsenal, who host struggling Hull, have won 18 of their past 19 Premier League games against promoted sides.
Things looking up for Spurs
The doom and gloom around Tottenham has lifted after a three-game winning streak in the Premier League under manager Roberto De Zerbi.
Less than three weeks ago Spurs, without a single win, propped up the division. They are now comfortably placed in mid-table.
Defender Archie Gray credits the spirit of the squad for the turnaround, which has the club just four points behind fourth-placed Chelsea.
"We all get on really well and you can see that out there on the pitch," he told SpursPlay. "Even with the celebration(s), all the subs are running to the players and they are little things that mean so much to us. That's the most important thing and why we've been improving."
Daniel Farke's Leeds are winless in their past five Premier League games and have scored just twice during that run, slipping to 12th in the table.

item.title: Australian T20 star Chris Lynn banned for cocaine use
item.description:
Big-hitting Australian Twenty20 specialist Chris Lynn has served a one-month ban for using cocaine and completed a substance abuse program, England's Cricket Regulator revealed Friday.
The all-time leading run-scorer in the Big Bash League tested positive during a routine anti-doping test on July 18 during the T20 Blast Finals Day in England.
He was a Northamptonshire player at the time, with England's Cricket Regulator only revealing the outcome on Friday.
"The Cricket Regulator has imposed a one-month suspension on former Northamptonshire Steelbacks cricketer Chris Lynn," it said. "The period of suspension has now been served."
Lynn, 36, tested positive for low levels of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, and admitted the charge.
His ban was reduced from three months after he completed a rehabilitation program and the regulator agreed it was out-of-competition use and not related to sporting performance.
Lynn played 18 T20s for Australia and four one-dayers.
Australian media said he was poised to join the Melbourne Renegades for this season's Big Bash League which gets underway next month.

item.title: Bournemouth stay perfect in Europa League as Milan lose again
item.description:
Bournemouth extended their perfect Europa League record on Thursday as they came from behind to win 3-1 at 10-man Sparta Prague, while Ruben Amorim's AC Milan suffered a third defeat in four matches.
Gambian Ebrima Singhateh ran from his own half to score a fine individual goal as Sparta took the lead in the Czech Republic after Bournemouth midfielder Lewis Cook hit the post with a first-half penalty.
Sparta had Tobias Guddal sent off before half-time and Bournemouth equalised through Tyler Adams on 57 minutes.
Evanilson steered the Cherries ahead nine minutes from time and Rayan bagged a late third as Bournemouth's substitutes fired the newcomers to a fourth successive victory in Europe.
Marco Rose's side have won each of their past seven matches in all competitions ahead of a Premier League trip to Ipswich this weekend.
"It's a big achievement and we have to continue, we need to stay alert, sharp," Rose told TNT Sports.
"It's up to us to use this momentum. Everyone tries to beat us, if we get in a comfort zone just a little bit we get in trouble."
Milan lost 2-0 at home to Ferencvaros as the Hungarians kept pace with Bournemouth, maintaining their 100 percent record in Europe.
Haiti international Lenny Joseph struck twice in the second half at San Siro to earn Ferencvaros a deserved win over the seven-time European champions despite having Bamidele Yusuf sent off.
"We gifted opportunities, made stupid errors. We were not prepared to play football tonight," Amorim told Sky Sport.
"I don't want to lie to my players. We cannot play like this in front of our own fans. It was a very poor performance."
Milan are languishing outside the top 24 with just three points at the halfway stage of the league phase.
"I won't give up on this competition. As long as we're not mathematically out of it, we'll keep fighting," Amorim added.
Benfica top the standings ahead of Bournemouth on goal difference after a 3-1 win at home to Lech Poznan, with Rafa Silva, Gianluca Prestianni and Georgiy Sudakov on the scoresheet for the Portuguese giants.
Bayer Leverkusen dropped their first points as they lost 1-0 at home to a Marseille team that had lost their first three matches.
Crystal Palace snatched a 1-1 draw at home to Hoffenheim as Japanese midfielder Daichi Kamada levelled in stoppage time.
Alexander Prass gave Hoffenheim an early lead at Selhurst Park and Palace lost Adam Wharton to a second yellow card before Kamada rescued a point for Pierre Sage's struggling side.
Palace, last season's UEFA Conference League winners, have five points from four outings in the Europa League but sit in the Premier League's relegation zone, just behind Manchester United on goal difference.
Sunderland, who have more points in Europe than the Premier League, saw their unbeaten Europa League start ended in a 2-0 home loss to Dinamo Zagreb.
"We are unlucky because we created many chances but it wasn't enough but sometimes it's like this," Sunderland manager Regis Le Bris told TNT Sports.
"Sometimes you go on a poor run, but we are still competitive, the players tried until the end."
Celtic picked up their first points with a thrilling 3-2 win over Besiktas as Camilo Duran came off the bench and netted twice for Martin O'Neill's side in Glasgow.
Teun Koopmeiners and Randal Kolo Muani scored for Juventus in their 2-1 win at AZ Alkmaar, lifting the Italians up to 10 points.
In the Conference League, Brighton edged past Getafe 1-0 in Spain courtesy of a second-half Malick Yalcouye header.
The Seagulls are two points behind the leading quartet of Lugano, Panathinaikos, Twente and Monaco, who have won all three of their games.
Four-time European champions Ajax thrashed Midtjylland 6-1 in Denmark, while Hearts remain without a win after losing 3-1 away to Thun.

item.title: We are running out of time
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest stark warning regarding our country’s rapidly fading demographic dividend should not be taken lightly, and must be treated with the seriousness it warrants.
For two decades, state planners have casually boasted about our youthful population as if economic prosperity were an automatic guarantee. Yet, as new data confirms, the window of demographic opportunity is closing at an alarming pace.
With our country set to transition into an "ageing" society next year and an "aged" nation by 2051, Bangladesh is running out of time. Failing to transform our young population into a highly skilled, productively employed workforce before the dependency ratio flips is an existential policy failure.
While there are numerous reasons for why we have essentially failed to capitalize on the gift that is our demographic dividend, it can primarily be attributed to systemic misdirection.
Over 84% of our workforce remains trapped in informal employment, where low wages, non-existent social protections, and minimal productivity reign.
Another notable failure is our inability to empower women, with female labour force participation languishing at a dismal 38% and effectively locking out half the nation's potential productivity.
Instead of building a knowledge-based economy capable of generating high-value formal jobs, successive policy failures have left our youth under-skilled, underemployed, and ill-prepared for what the future holds.
It is time to abandon rhetoric and immediately execute a comprehensive demographic strategy to make the most of the time we do have left.
The clock is ticking, and the window is closer to being shut than most realize. Failure to act now means our demographic dividend permanently collapsing into a demographic disaster.

item.title: Nourishing our future
item.description:
We certainly appreciate the government’s plan to dramatically expand the national school feeding program -- scaling coverage from 3.1 million to 11 million government primary school students across the country.
This is a deeply commendable initiative. Addressing primary education through the twin lenses of nutritional security and classroom retention is a progressive, essential strategy, and we can only hope for more decisions such as this.
In a country where child stunting, poverty, and post-primary dropouts remain severe challenges and have compromised our future, providing age-appropriate, quality meals in partnership with global experts like the World Food Program can transform the educational trajectory of millions of young citizens.
Indeed, the government correctly recognizes that learning outcomes cannot be separated from basic physical well-being. A hungry child cannot focus on foundational education.
Furthermore, incorporating community participation, specifically training local mothers in hygienic food preparation and distribution, adds a thoughtful layer of social empowerment and local oversight.
What is needed now is transparent implementation and execution of these plans. It is only then will this initiative boost attendance, combat malnutrition, safeguard child health, and foster genuine community ownership in our public education system.
Bangladesh’s policy landscape is littered with well-intentioned welfare schemes that stumbled as a result of corruption and disregard. Expanding coverage nearly fourfold will not be as simple as announcing the intention to do so.
Providing 11 million children with daily nourishment could be transformational for our country, but we must move swiftly from promises to implementation, ensuring that no child in Bangladesh is forced to choose between an empty stomach and an education.
The government has outlined a vision that deserves wholehearted public support. Now, it must deliver.

item.title: A historic first: Abdul El-Sayed’s senate victory against all the big guns
item.description:
The American people have once again demonstrated that, in a democracy, the ultimate source of political power rests with voters -- not billionaires, wealthy interest groups or even the president of the United States.
The projected victory of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s US Senate election on November 3, 2026 is a remarkable demonstration of this principle. Despite sustained personal attacks, religious and racial prejudice, enormous financial pressure, and political maneuvering, El-Sayed defeated Republican candidate Mike Rogers in a closely watched contest. This makes him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
This outcome represents much more than an individual electoral success. It is a significant challenge to the influence of money, political establishment, and divisive rhetoric in American democracy.
El-Sayed entered the contest promising to transform politics by returning power to ordinary people and challenging a system in which wealthy donors and powerful interest groups exercise disproportionate influence.
A physician and former public health leader, with a brilliant track record of delivering health services, El-Sayed brought a distinctive perspective to the campaign. His understanding of the everyday problems facing American families, combined with his ability to communicate practical solutions, distinguished him from his opponents.
Rather than allowing the campaign to become dominated by personal attacks, he consistently returned to a few central messages: Putting money back into people's pockets, getting money out of politics, and ensuring healthcare for all.
He repeatedly said that America is big enough for all of us -- it does not matter how you pray or not pray at all. He said, many are not the reason for the increase in gas price. It is the wrong policies of the president that has made the lives worse for the average American.
His campaign slogan captured the concerns of ordinary voters. People should not have to struggle simply to buy groceries, purchase essential medicines, fill their cars with petrol, or send their children to school. These are basic necessities, he argued, and a prosperous country such as the United States should be able to make them affordable.
El-Sayed also made his opposition to unconditional American military assistance to Israel a central part of his political position. He argued that public money should be invested in the needs of American communities rather than supporting military actions that have caused immense suffering to Palestinians.
He did not support any funding to Israel that has committed genocide and war crime in Gaza. His position was politically controversial, but he maintained that voters had the right to demand accountability over how their tax money was spent.
Personal attacks and religious prejudice
Perhaps the most extraordinary feature of the campaign was the intensity of the attacks directed at El-Sayed by President Donald Trump. Instead of concentrating exclusively on policy differences, Trump repeatedly targeted the candidate's Muslim faith, name, and background.
Among the expressions Trump used were “radical jihadist,” “jihadist” and, “Muslim Brotherhood member.” He also accused El-Sayed of being “on the side of the terrorists” and told him to “go back to where he came from,” although he was born in Michigan. On another occasion, Trump deliberately called him “Mohammed” and declared: “I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want.”
Trump further suggested that El-Sayed would represent a security threat in the Senate, saying that he would be the only senator required to pass through a metal detector. El-Sayed responded with a sharp retort: He would be willing to go through a metal detector if Trump would agree to go through a lie detector.
Trump also attempted to associate El-Sayed with the imposition of Sharia law, invoked the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, and suggested that Jewish and Black voters would be foolish to support him.
Such statements raise serious questions about Islamophobia, racial stereotyping, and religious prejudice in American electoral politics. Political disagreement is a legitimate part of democracy, and candidates must be open to criticism of their policies and public statements. However, portraying a fellow American as a terrorist or a foreigner without credible evidence is fundamentally different from challenging his political program.
A candidate's religion or ethnic background should never be treated as evidence of disloyalty or a threat to national security. The American electorate's response to these attacks will be closely examined, particularly because the campaign attempted to make religious identity a defining issue in a contest that should have centred on public policy and the future of Michigan.
A campaign against corporate financial influence
Another major challenge facing El-Sayed was the extraordinary financial power deployed against him during the Democratic primary. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), through its affiliated political action committee, the United Democracy Project, spent close to $30 million supporting his primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, and opposing El-Sayed. This was reported as the largest investment the organization had made in a single electoral race.
El-Sayed nevertheless won the Democratic nomination. He repeatedly criticized the influence of outside money in elections and argued that political representatives should be accountable to their constituents rather than wealthy and corporate donors and powerful lobbying organizations.
The scale of the financial imbalance was striking. During the primary campaign, El-Sayed described himself as being outspent by approximately 11 to one. His ability to overcome that disadvantage demonstrated the strength of grassroots mobilisation and the appeal of a campaign focused on the cost of living, healthcare, and political accountability.
His victory should not, however, be interpreted as a rejection or approval of any particular religious or ethnic community. Criticism of a foreign government's policies and opposition to military assistance are legitimate political positions. The central democratic question is whether elected representatives should be influenced by ordinary voters or by powerful financial interests.
A broader message from Muslim and minority voters
El-Sayed's victory is part of a wider political development involving Muslim and minority representation in the United States. Muslim Americans have increasingly participated in electoral politics, sought public office and demanded that their concerns be addressed as part of the national political debate.
The election also demonstrated that candidates should not be judged by religious identity or ethnic background. Voters are entitled to evaluate their representatives on competence, integrity, policy positions and their ability to improve people's lives.
Both Congress Women Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) and Rashida Tlaib (Michigan) faced vicious racial and religious vilifications but have been re-elected with increased votes.
The attempt to use anti-Muslim rhetoric as an electoral weapon may therefore have produced the opposite of its intended effect.
Rather than allowing religious prejudice to dominate the debate, El-Sayed kept returning to issues that affect people across religious, racial and ethnic boundaries: Household expenses, healthcare, education, employment and the influence of money in politics.
Very wisely, he did not respond to any unhelpful distracting personal attacks despite repeated incitement by the President and his opponent.
A changing political landscape in Washington
The implications of the 2026 midterm elections extend beyond Michigan. Election projections indicate that Democrats have gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. If counting and certification are completed, this will significantly change the political balance in Washington and create a stronger congressional check on President Trump's administration.
A divided government -- or one in which the president's party lacks control of Congress -- can have substantial consequences for legislation, public expenditure, foreign policy and executive accountability. Congressional oversight will become particularly important in areas where presidential decisions face strong political or constitutional objections.
There is also a significant development concerning American assistance to Israel. On November 3, Trump said that the United States would end its approximately $4 billion in annual aid to Israel after 2026, while continuing arms sales and other forms of assistance if required. He described Israel as sufficiently prosperous to manage without the annual funding.
However, the existing US-Israel assistance agreement runs through 2028, and the practical and legal implications of ending the assistance earlier remain to be clarified. The announcement is particularly noteworthy given the growing public debate in the United States about the war in Gaza and the use of American taxpayer money.
People's power is the ultimate decider
Abdul El-Sayed's victory offers an important lesson for democracies everywhere. Money can purchase advertising, political influence and access to powerful institutions, but it cannot automatically purchase public trust. Presidential endorsement, political intimidation and personal attacks cannot guarantee electoral success.
The people of Michigan have sent a message that their economic security, access to healthcare and political future matter more than attempts to divide them through religion, race or ethnicity. El-Sayed's success also demonstrates that a candidate can challenge powerful interests by presenting a clear program, maintaining consistency and building a broad grassroots movement.
His victory does not mean that the problems of American democracy have been solved. The influence of wealthy donors, political lobbying, racial discrimination and religious prejudice will remain subjects of public debate. Nor does one election guarantee that campaign promises will be fulfilled. El-Sayed will now face the difficult task of translating his commitments into legislation and practical improvements in people's lives.
Nevertheless, his achievement is historic. It demonstrates that the power of ordinary people, when mobilised around shared concerns and democratic principles, can overcome formidable political and financial obstacles.
Ultimately, democracy belongs to the people. No president, billionaire, lobby group or political establishment can permanently stand above the collective voice of an informed electorate.
Professor Dr Shahjahan Khan OAM is an Emeritus Professor at the University of Southern Queensland, Australia; an Expatriate Fellow of the Bangladesh Academy of Sciences; and former Vice-Chancellor of the Asian University of Bangladesh, Dhaka.
