item.title: Journalist Robiul denies touching allegation, says Pori Moni snatched his phone
item.description:
Journalist Robiul Hossain, a multimedia reporter at the daily Samakal, has denied the allegation that he touched film actress Pori Moni. Instead, he has accused the actress of snatching his mobile phone.

Robiul Hossain told Prothom Alo that Pori Moni hurled abusive language at him and threatened to kill him. He said all of this was captured on video.

Last Thursday, at a Dhaka court premises, film actress Pori Moni accused journalist Robiul Hossain of touching her. Later, she verbally abused him in front of journalists.

Pori Moni went to the Dhaka Chief Judicial Magistrate Court premises on Thursday morning to surrender and seek bail in a case filed by businessman Nasir Uddin Mahmud.

Nasir Uddin Mahmud filed the case at a Dhaka court on 6 July 2022. In the case, he alleged that Pori Moni and her associates vandalised the Savar Boat Club on the night of 9 June 2021 and assaulted him and threatened to kill him.

‘How dare he touch me!’ Enraged Pori Moni at court premises

Earlier, Pori Moni had filed a case at Savar Police Station against Nasir Uddin and others, accusing them of rape and attempted murder in connection with the incident. Testimony is being recorded in that case. Nasir Uddin is out on bail.

After learning that Pori Moni would appear in court in Nasir Uddin's case, journalists from different media outlets gathered there on Thursday.

At around 11:40 am, as Pori Moni got out of her car and headed towards the courtroom, journalists tried to take photographs and videos. This led to a scuffle between them and her security personnel.

At this point, allegations emerged that Pori Moni had snatched the mobile phone of Samakal multimedia reporter Robiul Hossain. Robiul said Pori Moni herself had taken his phone. He also said that security personnel accompanying Pori Moni broke the tripod he was using to record videos. He later took the phone back from her.

What happened in the lift, both sides give their accounts

Pori Moni gave her explanation of what happened while getting into the lift. She told Prothom Alo, “As I was getting into the lift, someone would not let me in. There is a schedule at the court, and I had to reach there on time. Someone pushed a mobile phone past the side of my head, and there was a stand attached to it. The lift door could not close because of the phone. I moved the phone away with my hand. After moving it, I felt that someone had grabbed my hand.”

Pori Moni said, “I know how the two people who hold me touch me. This was the kind of grip that causes pain, as if someone was clawing at me. I felt pain. I also thought, why did Ratul (one of the people accompanying me) hold me like that? When I looked, I saw that boy (journalist Robiul Hossain).”

Pori Moni further said, “I remembered his face. After getting bail, I kept looking for him as I walked around the court premises. After getting bail in the dock and coming downstairs, I turned my head and saw him. Then I said, ‘Come here.’ I called him using informal and disrespectful language. When I asked why he had held my hand like that, I then heard him saying, ‘Apa, my tripod has been broken.’ At that moment, I felt like burying him in the ground. For some reason, my hand did not rise, even though I was about to raise it.”

Denying Pori Moni's allegation, Robiul Hossain said he did not get into the lift. He was standing in a corner and recording video while people were getting into the lift. He said it was not true that the lift could not close because of his mobile phone and tripod.

Robiul further said, “I do not know whether the lift was unable to close because of a camera person or a lawyer who was already inside it. As Pori Moni was entering the lift, she pulled my phone away. Why would I block her path while she was getting into the lift? I never created any obstruction in her way.”

Responding to the allegation that he had touched Pori Moni, Robiul said, “She is talking about being touched, but I was holding my mobile phone and tripod in my left hand. My right hand is completely out of use (Robiul Hossain’s right hand is congenitally smaller than his left, and three fingers are missing; he cannot perform normal activities with this hand). There was no way I could have touched her with this hand. Those who saw me in person know this.”

Robiul said, “I cannot say who touched her (Pori Moni). Her own security personnel were with her in that lift.”

Pori Moni granted bail on Tk 500 bond

Tensions flare again after leaving court

After the hearing, Pori Moni secured bail on a bond of Tk 500. However, the situation became tense again as she left the court.

Journalists alleged that Pori Moni's security personnel pushed them. At one point, Pori Moni approached journalist Robiul Hossain, called him over and hurled abusive language at him. Witnesses alleged that people accompanying her also engaged in heated exchanges with journalists.

Describing the situation as they left the court, Robiul told Prothom Alo that one of the people accompanying Pori Moni (later identified as Turan Munshi) first asked him about touching her in the lift. Pori Moni then approached him herself.

Robiul told Prothom Alo, “She (Pori Moni) was hurling abusive language at me. As she was leaving, she threatened to kill me. Everything that was done to me at that time is on video. Everyone has seen it.”

Arrest warrant issued against actress Pori Moni

Journalists, another person seeking justice injured in scuffle

Journalists were not the only ones injured in the scuffle at the court premises that day; a person who had come to court seeking justice was also injured. The man, named Sujan Chandra Mani Das, sustained a head injury that left him bleeding. His brother alleged that he was injured after being pushed by Pori Moni's security personnel.

Besides, Jago News reporter Ashikuzzaman and multimedia reporter Abdullah Al Kawsar, Agamir Shomoy reporter Siam Hossain, and Shah Riaz of Times Today were injured. Some of the injured journalists also received treatment at hospitals.

The Digital Reporters Forum (DRF) has condemned the incident. In a press release sent out last Thursday, the organisation said allegations had emerged that film actress Pori Moni behaved discourteously towards journalists, hurled abusive language at them and harassed them at the Dhaka Chief Judicial Magistrate Court premises. Subsequently, allegations were also received that her personal security personnel assaulted, pushed and beat journalists and ordinary people who had come to court seeking justice.

The DRF strongly condemned and protested the injury and harassment of at least five journalists while performing their professional duties.

In its statement, the organisation further said that, as an actress, Pori Moni obstructing journalists from performing their professional duties at an important and sensitive place like a court, behaving discourteously towards them or allowing her security personnel to harass them was in no way acceptable. It also said the injury of ordinary people who had come to court was a matter of grave concern.

The DRF believes that such behaviour towards journalists is not only an attack on their professional dignity but also a threat to the environment necessary for independent journalism and the media to perform their duties.

It has demanded a fair and impartial investigation into the allegations against Pori Moni and her security personnel, identification of those responsible and legal action against them.

item.title: Miscreants set bus on fire in Baridhara
item.description:
Miscreants have set fire to a passenger bus operated by Boishakhi Paribahan on Pragati Sarani in the Baridhara area of the capital. No casualties have been reported, police said.

The bus was set ablaze in Baridhara's J Block at around 5.45 pm on Friday.

According to Bhatara police, the Boishakhi Paribahan bus operates on the Savar–Notun Bazar route. Shortly after the bus dropped off passengers in Baridhara in the evening, two or three miscreants suddenly set fire to the bus and fled the scene.

After being alerted, two units of the Baridhara Fire Station rushed to the spot and extinguished the blaze. The passengers managed to get out safely before the fire could spread. No one was injured.

Police also said that no clear CCTV (closed-circuit television) footage of the incident was available from the immediate vicinity. They are examining footage from surrounding areas in an effort to identify those responsible.

Bhatara police station officer-in-charge Mohammad Mazharul Islam said that after the Fire Service had extinguished the fire, a police team went to the scene and had the bus removed.

The driver and his assistant were taken to the police station for questioning in connection with the incident.

Police are working to bring those involved in setting fire to the bus to justice, the OC added.

item.title: Defeated forces of 7 Nov turned the country into a subservient state in name of Grand Alliance: PM
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has wished that the revolutionary spirit of 7 November serve as the inspiration and guiding force for building the future Bangladesh.

He made the wish in a message on the occasion of the Historic National Revolution and Solidarity Day to be observed tomorrow, Saturday.

Tarique Rahman said on 7 November 1975, the soldiers and people of Bangladesh united to thwart all conspiracies against the country's independence and sovereignty.

The historic 7 November was a defining moment in the nation's history, when the friends and foes of Bangladesh were clearly identified, he said.

He said a saying deserves particular consideration in discussing Bangladesh's Liberation War and the various historic milestones of the nation: “Those who remain preoccupied with the past are blind in one eye, while those who forget the past are blind in both eyes.”

It is, therefore, neither appropriate to remain absorbed in the past all the time nor is it wise to ignore the lessons of history while charting the course for the future, said Tarique Rahman adding that both approaches would be historical mistakes.

“I believe that the historic 7 November, 1975 was a defining date in determining Bangladesh's course,” he said.

Those who sought to turn Bangladesh into a subservient state, those who wanted to deprive the people of their democratic and political rights and establish one-party authoritarian rule and those who sought to undermine the glory of the armed forces, the symbol of the nation's valour, courage and honour, were defeated through the historic revolution of the patriotic soldiers and people on that day, he said.

The Prime Minister said history bears the witness that the defeated forces of 7 November, 1975 later united under the banner of the Grand Alliance and turned the country into a subservient state following a prolonged course of conspiracy.

Tarique Rahman said they carried out the planned massacre of military personnel at the BDR Headquarters in Pilkhana, undermining the glory and dignity of the armed forces.

They also deprived the people of their voting rights and democratic and political freedoms, establishing a fascist regime in the country, he said.

Finally, after more than a decade and a half, the country was freed from fascism through a bloody mass uprising led by brave students and people, at the cost of thousands of martyrs, said the premier.

“The War of 1971 was fought to achieve independence. The struggle of 2024 was to safeguard the independence of the country and its people,” said Tarique Rahman.

Just as people from all walks of life took to the streets in 2024 to defend the freedom of the country and its people, the soldiers and civilians had also united and taken to the streets in 1975 to thwart all conspiracies against the country's independence and sovereignty, he added.

“Our foremost commitment on this year's 7 November should be to ensure that no one can ever again deprive the country and its people of their rights or turn Bangladesh into a subservient state. National unity is essential to fulfill this commitment,” he said.

Given Bangladesh's socio-economic, geographical and political realities, preserving national unity requires us to embrace wholeheartedly the spirit of the soldiers' and people's revolution of 7 November, he said.

Tarique Rahman said the Liberation War of 1971, the soldiers' and people's revolution of 7 November, 1975 against subservient forces, the anti-autocracy movement of 1990, and the anti-fascist mass uprising of 2024 - all these revolutions and uprisings at different junctures in our history have been driven by one common aspiration: to build a self-reliant, secure and welfare-oriented state in an independent Bangladesh by ensuring all democratic and political rights of the people.

“On this historic day, commemorating the 7 November, 1975 revolution of the soldiers and people, who were fought to thwart conspiracies against Bangladesh's independence and sovereignty and to protect the democratic rights of its people, let the resolute voice of the patriotic and democracy-loving people ring out: Neither Delhi nor Pindi, nor any other country; Bangladesh comes first,” he said.

He wished every success to all programmes organised nationally to mark 7 November.

item.title: HSC supplementary exams: Allegations of extra fees for form submission
item.description:
The process of filling in forms for supplementary examinations of candidates, who failed in a maximum of two subjects (excluding the fourth subject) in this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations, is currently under way.

However, allegations have emerged that candidates are being charged extra fees in the name of form submission.

In this situation, the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee has said that no candidate may be charged any additional fee for filling in examination forms.

If this instruction is not followed, legal action will be taken against the heads of the institutions concerned and the institutions themselves. The committee issued this warning in a notice dated 5 November.

HSC: Students who fail in up to 2 subjects can retake exams on 1 Dec

The supplementary examinations will begin on 1 December. Both regular and irregular candidates will be eligible to sit them. The opportunity is being offered to candidates who failed in a maximum of two subjects.

Form submission for the examinations began on 5 November and will continue until 9 November. The deadline for payment of fees is 10 November.

The form submission fee has been set at Tk 125 for each theoretical paper or subject and Tk 25 for each practical paper or subject. In addition, the examination centre fee is Tk 450.

At present, if a candidate fails in one or more subjects in public examinations such as the SSC and HSC, they must sit the examinations again a year later, in the following year.

HSC result 2026: Worst performance in 22 years

In that case, they may sit examinations only in the subjects they failed, or choose to retake all subjects. However, students have to wait a full year because they failed in just one or two subjects.

This time, the education authorities have decided to hold another examination within a month for candidates who failed in a maximum of two subjects.

The results of this year’s HSC and equivalent examinations were published on 31 October. A total of 422,905 candidates failed in one or two subjects. Of them, 298,040 failed in one subject and 124,865 failed in two subjects.

item.title: People will not allow Awami League in politics anymore: Home Minister
item.description:
The people of the country will never allow Awami League to practice politics again, said Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed.

He made the statement as the chief guest while addressing the 104th annual religious conference of Al-Jamiatul Islamia Azizul Uloom Babunagar Madrasa in Fatikchhari, Chattogram, ahead of Jummah prayers on Friday. The second day of the conference was presided over by Shah Muhibbullah Babunagari, Ameer of Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh.

In his address, the home minister said, "We agree on one point. The people of this country will never again allow those who carried out mass killings, shed the blood of religious scholars for 16 long years and turned mosques into places of bloodshed to engage in politics. We want to take the country out of the state governance policies of fascist Sheikh Hasina and restore the spirit of the Liberation War and the country's previous state policies. We will once again incorporate firm faith and trust in Almighty Allah into the Constitution’s preamble and the principles of state governance."

The home minister continued, "We have been freed from the hands of anti-Islamic forces. Over the past 16 to 17 years, nearly 3,000 people have been victims of enforced disappearance and torture. I was one of them. People have faced oppression and torture in various ways. We want to restore the dignity we have lost."

Salahuddin Ahmed said those who were doing politics in the name of religion had no connection with Islam through their actions. They were only creating disorder in the country. He called for governing the state and conducting politics by following the fundamental principles of Islam.

Referring to BNP Chairperson Khaleda Zia, the home minister said people had suffered for a long time because of injustice, misrule and corruption. He also remarked that even someone like Khaleda Zia had to die without receiving proper medical treatment.

On Awami League's return to politics, Salahuddin Ahmed said those who had stood against democracy and fled the country in the face of the mass uprising will not be allowed to engage in politics in Bangladesh again.

Speaking about the July mass uprising and the July Charter, the home minister said the government is committed to implementing the charter formulated through the election. At the same time, Islamic values will be reflected in the Constitution, he added.

Addressing ongoing demonstrators, he said, "To those creating confusion in the name of protests, I want to say, criticise us, but let it be constructive criticism. You can cooperate with the government, but do not conspire against the people of the country."

The home minister added, "We want to keep this country united and achieve economic development and prosperity, increase exports, create employment and generate electricity in every sector. We will gradually move towards prosperity, taking everyone along. The economic condition of the people of this country must improve. The living standards of all religious scholars and students of Qawmi madrasas must also improve."

State Minister for Religious Affairs Shamim Kaiser Lincoln, local Member of Parliament Sarwar Alamgir, Raozan MP Gias Uddin Quader Chowdhury, Rangunia MP Hummam Quader Chowdhury, Chattogram Deputy Commissioner Zahidul Islam Miah and Chattogram Superintendent of Police Masud Alam, among others, were present on the occasion.

item.title: Hasi’s life is a struggle, but she keeps smiling
item.description:
It was a leisurely afternoon on 24 October, the final day of the Durga Puja holidays. Walking past a mosque and along the footpath beside it, I entered the Dhanmondi Lake area. People were strolling around here and there. After walking a little further, I sat down on a circular seating area beside a bridge. A few people were sitting scattered about, some in groups and others alone. Among them was a woman sitting by herself, with a square basket and a bag beside her. Her basket contained a small assortment of items, including plastic toys, hair clips and round caps.

‘Do you sell these things?’ I asked. She nodded in the affirmative.

‘Do you sit here every day?’

This time, she gave a longer answer. She did not come to this spot every day; instead, she went around selling her goods. She frequently visits Road Nos 11 and 28 of Dhanmondi. Her children accompanied her, too. On holidays, an organisation held classes for street children on this side of the lake. She had brought her children there to attend the classes. After the lessons, the teachers had taken the young students to have a meal. She was waiting for them to return.

As we talked, I learnt that her name was Bina Akter Hasi, 30. She lived in Hazaribagh, in the capital, with her 13-year-old son, Mohammad Hasan, and five-year-old daughter, Mariam Jannat.

“I have been working since childhood to make ends meet. I started washing pots and pans when I was four. I have been earning my living through hard work ever since. Pens and papers may run out but my story of suffering will never end. I have endured so much hardship,” she said.

As Hasi spoke, a kitten climbed into her lap. She explained that it was her pet. At one point in our conversation, her children returned. Her wait was over. She was now ready to take them along and resume selling the goods in her basket, this time around Dhanmondi Road No. 28. I accompanied them.

Lost while searching for her mother

Hasi said she could not remember the names of her parents or siblings, or the address of her family home. All she remembered was that they had lived in a village. They would get off a boat and then take a rickshaw to reach their home.

After her father married again, her mother brought the children to Dhaka and took up domestic work in a household.

Her mother subsequently placed four-year-old Hasi in another family's care as a domestic worker. One day, while trying to find her mother, she left the house and lost her way. For some reason, she also forgot her own name. She thought it might have been Bina.

She was then taken in by a teacher in Old Dhaka, who gave her the name ‘Hasi’. She stayed in that household until her adolescence. Later, she found shelter in the home of a woman in Kamrangirchar.

Married life, then left adrift by her husband's death

In Kamrangirchar, Hasi found work at a plastic factory. The woman who had given her shelter arranged her marriage to an orphaned young man named Billal, who worked as an electrician.

One day, Billal died from electrocution while at work.

“Life was good after we got married. My hardship had eased a little. I thought perhaps Allah had finally mended my broken fate. But when he died, suffering returned to my life,” Hasi said.

At the time of her husband's death, their son was seven years old and their daughter was just one and a half months old.

After her marriage, she did not need to work outside the home. Following her husband's death, she would leave the infant girl with her son and go to work in people's homes. But the boy was unable to look after his baby sister. Hasi subsequently began taking her daughter along to work. However, because the child would urinate unexpectedly, no one was willing to employ her.

Hasi then spent some time working in construction, selling tea from a flask, and later found a job at a factory in Rayerbazar. When the factory shut down during the Covid-19 pandemic, she lost her job.

During this period, Hasi would come to Dhanmondi with her neighbours in the hope of receiving assistance. At one point, after seeing children selling goods on the streets, she began selling luchni (thick clothes sewed together to hold hot utensils in the kitchen). She bought luchni (potholders) and majuni (scrubbers) worth Tk 300 from Chawkbazar and started going from place to place to sell them, accompanied by her son.

How well do they sell?

During the two and a half hours I spent with the family, I did not see them sell a single item. Hasi, however, said they sell goods worth an average of Tk 300 a day. Their sales were limited because they had very little capital. Moreover, as Hasi was unwell, she could no longer walk around as much as she used to. Her son now went around on foot to sell the goods.

From this month, their monthly house rent had increased to Tk 4,000. Hasi said she was unable to pay the full rent in any month.

A couple from Dhanmondi, who had initially bought luchni from her, continued to help her in various ways. Hasi said, “Sir and Madam admitted me to hospital and arranged treatment for me.”

Several times during our conversation, Hasi became emotional.

“People suffer for some days, but my suffering began the moment I was born. My children are suffering, too. I just want them to be able to eat a little better,” she said.

* Naznin Akhter, Senior Correspondent, Prothom Alo

item.title: Dhaka’s monorail plans: 2 corridors targeted for completion by 2030
item.description:
The government is moving ahead with plans to introduce two monorail corridors in the city by 2030, with consultants now working on detailed designs following completion of a pre-feasibility study.

"The proposed monorail systems are expected to expand the capital's public transport network by offering commuters an environmentally friendly, sustainable and efficient mode of transportation, particularly in areas where passengers' pressure is high," Additional Executive Director of the Dhaka Transport Coordination Authority (DTCA) Md Moshiur Rahman told BSS today, Friday.

He said the proposed monorail corridors will have opportunities to connect with existing and planned metro rail and other public transport services, particularly to improve last-mile connectivity for metro rail passengers.

The consultants of Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) have completed the pre-feasibility study, while the designs would be completed during the stipulated period.

The final two corridors will be selected based on comprehensive technical, economic and environmental assessments, including their passenger demand, potential benefits and financial viability.

Metro rail or monorail: Which is more practical?

The DTCA conducted traffic-modelling surveys across the capital to assess passenger demand and subsequently shared the findings with BUET consultants for analysis, he added.

Moshiur Rahman said the DTCA signed an agreement titled "Consultancy Service for Pre-Feasibility Study of Monorail Alignment Integration with Mass Transit Networks in Dhaka Metropolitan Region" to assess the prospects of introducing the system.

The Bureau of Research, Testing and Consultation (BRTC) of BUET had completed the pre-feasibility study, while experts are now preparing the detailed designs, which are expected to be submitted within six months as per the deal.

According to project details, the government allocated Tk 75.7 billion from its revenue budget for conducting the pre-feasibility study and preparing detailed designs for the two proposed monorail corridors.

The study aims to assess the feasibility of introducing a monorail-based public transport system in Dhaka and identify ways to integrate it effectively with existing and planned metro rail and other public transport networks.

Under the Updated Revised Strategic Transport Plan, five monorail corridors spanning around 79.4 kilometres have been proposed. A preferred corridor is expected to be selected within three months, while the full study is scheduled to be completed within six months.

It said the five routes were identified based on the lack of accessible bus services to serve as feeder services for mass rapid transit (MRT) lines.

The five initial proposed corridors are: Airport-Bashundhara via Purbachal and Jolshiri (25.2 km); Middle Badda-Bhulta (14.6 km); Rampura-Demra (10.3 km); Mohammadpur-Postogola (11.7 km); and Airport-Savar via Uttara Centre (17.6 km), it said.

The monorail route 8 is suggested from TSC to Kamrangirchar with nine stations, while route 10 is proposed from Alubdi to West Agargaon or Shyamoli with 10 stations, and route 13 from Paltan to Sadarghat or Jhilmil with six or 11 stations.

Talking to BSS, a member of the BUET consultation team said as they were assigned to conduct the pre-feasibility study covering the metropolitan area, per-kilometre population, catchment areas of stations, inaccessibility of public transport, congested areas, depot site availability, and future scopes were reviewed to identify the corridors.

Metro rail extension to Kamalapur 85pc complete, service set to begin in July

The proposed monorail system would help develop an integrated, efficient and sustainable public transport network in the capital, he said.

The government-funded study will examine route alignments, potential station and depot locations, passenger demand, technical and structural suitability, economic viability, and environmental and social impacts.

As monorails generally operate on elevated structures, the DTCA is examining their potential to provide transport links in densely populated parts of Dhaka, where limited road space and other infrastructure constraints may pose challenges to developing conventional mass rapid transit systems.

The study will also evaluate construction costs, passenger-carrying capacity, operational expenses and the overall economic and social viability of the proposed system.

Local and non-resident Bangladeshi experts have been engaged as consultants to support the study.

The initiative follows the government's electoral pledge to introduce monorail services in Dhaka as part of its broader efforts to improve urban mobility and ease traffic congestion in the capital.

item.title: ‘I cannot make ends meet on under Tk 800 a day’
item.description:
Most of his hair has turned white, as have his moustache and beard. Wrinkles crease his forehead and his eyes are slightly sunken. A gentle smile lingers on his face, yet a shadow of uncertainty clouds his gaze.

His name is Sukumar Rabidas, now in his fifties. He lives in the Rabidas Polli of Faridpur town. For nearly 40 years, he has been crafting shoes and sandals, stitching and repairing worn-out footwear, dyeing and polishing shoes.

He works by the roadside in Moyrapatti, on the bank of the Kumar River, in front of a sanitary ware shop. His father and grandfather practiced the exact same trade. Sukumar learned the craft from his father, who had learned it from his own father. And so it has continued, down through the generations.

A conversation struck up with Sukumar by that very roadside one day. He sits down for work around 10:00 am and heads home at night, taking a brief midday break to eat lunch at home. "There is not much income," he says. "Some days I earn Tk 500, some days Tk 300. Even less on some days. It's a daily struggle to run the household..."

There are four members in Sukumar’s family. His wife, Shobha Rani Rabidas is a homemaker. His daughter Tumpa has completed her SSC examinations, while his son Manoj is in the eighth grade. Sukumar is the sole breadwinner in his family. He says that this financial hardship is not his alone, almost everyone in his profession faces the same situation.

Market flooded with machine-made shoes

People in this line of work did not always face such distress. Sukumar recalls, "Handmade shoes and sandals used to be in demand. Every month, people would place orders for five to 10 dozen pairs. But now the market is flooded with machine-made shoes and sandals..."

Nowadays, he receives orders for only about 18 to 20 pairs a month. Even then, not everyone who places an order comes back to pick them up. Some pay an advance and never return. He tries to sell them to other customers. Some find buyers, while others remain unsold for a long time.

According to Sukumar, he makes a profit of roughly Tk 100 per pair, earning around Tk 2000 a month from crafting new shoes. His main income comes from repairing, dyeing and polishing old shoes, which brings in about Tk 15,000 a month.

In total, he makes around Tk 17,000 monthly. Yet, as he puts it, even a very frugal household needs at least Tk 800 a day to get by. He therefore has to borrow money and buy groceries on credit from local shops. There is a cooperative society in their community from which he takes loans and repays them in weekly instalments. In Sukumar’s words, he is trapped in a cycle of debt.

Only four shoemakers left in Moyrapatti

Braving both scorching heat and rain, Sukumar has to sit out in the open by the roadside. "Our ancestors worked like this and we are carrying on in the same way," he says. "But it feels bad to sit and work by the roadside. Of course, I have never demanded that we be given a place to work. I have not heard that our fathers or grandfathers ever made such a demand either."

The number of people in this profession is also declining. Sukumar explains, "Young people today do not want to take up this profession. I see no interest among them in learning this trade. Some work in salons, while others take jobs at different shops in markets. Yet, during the Pakistan era, 20 to 25 cobblers from our community used to sit right here at Moyrapotti. For a long time after independence, the numbers remained roughly the same. But over the years, many passed away. Now, there are only four of us left in this neighborhood."

Sukumar does not want his son to enter this trade, nor does his son show any interest to follow in his forebears' footsteps. So why does he regret the decline in the number of people in the trade?

Sukumar says he has no regrets. Even if the numbers shrink, the profession will never completely vanish. As he puts it, "As long as our community exists, this profession will remain. Not everyone can afford to educate their children. Those who do not get an education will take up this trade."

Struggling to survive against all odds

A visit to Sukumar’s home in the Rabidas neighbourhood revealed a small, dilapidated house with an earthen floor, a tin roof and tin walls. He lives there with his wife and two children. There is a cooking area in one corner of the house. The toilet is shared, located some distance away.

A total of 47 families live in Rabidas Polli. Even holding onto this settlement required an uphill battle. Sukumar explains that they once lived on their own registered land in Haji Shariatullah Bazar. In 1965, the government acquired that land and relocated them here. Some portions of this land fell under government records. According to Sukumar, an eviction drive in 2012 demolished 13 houses, including his own, without offering any rehabilitation. "Yet, we didn't abandon the land," he says. "We gritted our teeth and stayed put. After filing a case and going through legal proceedings, we secured the right to live here through the district judge’s court."

Sukumar longs to break free from the poverty and deprivation endured across generations. He believes that only the government can truly step in and stand beside them.

Staying up late for the joy of making shoes

Despite all the hardship, Sukumar genuinely loves his work. Making a new pair of shoes gives him pleasure. He says, "This work demands total focus. When I sit working at home, I lose track of time. Sometimes it is already one or two in the morning. There are times when I have no orders, yet I stay up late making shoes simply because I enjoy it. I do not even think about whether I will be able to sell them..."
